events.text: Late summer, and the new house is not up. The walls have to be raised before the autumn rains or the whole year's work will melt back into mud, and the corner posts are still lying in the grass. But these are the eighteen days before autumn, and the old people say that in the days between the seasons the earth belongs to nobody but itself: no digging, no moving graves, no raising walls. The oldest woman on the lane has said it three times today. The clouds in the west say something else.

choices.text: Dig anyway: the rain will not wait

effects.log: You drive the spade in where the first post goes. It comes up full of yellow clay, very fine, and warm, warm as bread, and in the middle of the lump something beats, once, like a held breath let go. Under your feet the whole site seems to settle, the way a sleeper turns over. The posts go in that evening. The walls are up before the rain. The oldest woman on the lane will not speak to you for a week, and then, quietly, asks to hold some of the clay.

choices.text: Wait the eighteen days, and lose the walls to the rain

effects.log: You wait. The rain comes on the ninth day and the half-raised walls slump into the yard, and the neighbours shake their heads at you. On the nineteenth morning you start again from nothing. When the spade goes in, the clay under the site is warm, as if something had been lying there all this while, and had noticed you leaving it alone.

choices.text: Ask the village shaman what to do

effects.log: The shaman walks the site twice, sniffing, and says: bury a jar of new rice where the centre of the house will be, with a straw cap over it, "so whatever lives there has a roof before you do." You do it that evening. When the jar goes into the ground, the earth under your knees moves, once, like a held breath let go. You dig the posts in the next day and nothing goes wrong. Nothing at all goes wrong in that house for years.

events.text: The first full moon, and the farmers' band is going from yard to yard to stamp on the earth spirit: the little gong screaming, the hourglass drum, the big drum, the great gong booming, and everyone stamping in a ring so the spirit under the house will be soothed and the bad luck driven out. This year they have let you carry the small drum. In the old Kim house's yard, on the third stamp, the ground under your foot stamps back.

choices.text: Stamp again, harder, and see

effects.log: You stamp. The yard stamps back, a beat behind, deep down, like the big drum but underneath everything. Nobody else seems to notice. You stamp twice, and it stamps twice. The band moves on to the next house, and you have to be dragged, and all night you lie awake with your hand flat on the floor, waiting. Near dawn it gives one slow beat, like somebody saying goodnight.

choices.text: Lie down flat in the yard and listen

effects.log: You lie down on the frozen yard with your ear to the dirt, in front of the whole band. The grown-ups laugh. Under the earth, very far down, something is breathing, slow as the tide, and warm: you can feel the warm through your cheek. When you get up there is a patch of yard the shape of your face where the frost has melted. The old Kim grandmother looks at it for a long time.

choices.text: Give your New Year rice cake to the ground

effects.log: You do not know why. You take the rice cake the Kim house gave you, the good one, with honey in it, and press it into the dirt of the yard, and say sorry for the stamping. The ground is warm under your hand. The next morning the Kim grandmother finds the place, and the cake gone, and a little ring of grass green in the middle of winter, and tells the whole village it was you.

events.text: Your errand has brought you to a great ruined temple of the old kingdom: sixty-four foundation stones in the long grass where a wooden pagoda nine storeys high once stood, and in the middle the great centre stone, its socket full of rainwater. You are meant only to deliver a letter to the caretaker. But at midnight there are lanterns at the centre stone, and a rival sect's men with crowbars, levering it up to get at the relic box underneath. The ground shakes. The water in the socket turns gold.

choices.text: Stop the diggers

ok.log: You come out of the grass and it is short. The crowbars go into the dark, and so do the diggers, and the great stone settles back into its bed with a sound like a sigh. The gold in the socket fades slowly to rainwater again. In the morning the caretaker finds you asleep against the centre stone, and says the stone was warm all night, and that it has not been warm in six hundred years.

fail.log: There are more of them than you thought. You take a crowbar across the ribs and go down in the grass. And then the ground shakes again, hard, and the centre stone drops back into its bed by itself, so heavily the diggers are thrown off their feet, and they run. You lie there in the wet grass with the gold light going out of the socket, and you could swear the stone is breathing. (-8 health)

choices.text: Take the relic box yourself, before they do

effects.log: You get there first and lift out the box: bronze, the size of a loaf, and heavy, far heavier than gold. With every step away from the stone it gets heavier, until at the edge of the grass you are on your knees, and it weighs what a house weighs, and you understand that it is not the box. You carry it back. At the stone it weighs nothing at all. You put it back in the dark under the stone and the ground lets out a long breath.

choices.text: Shout them off, put the stone back, and sit on it until dawn

effects.log: You make enough noise for a whole sect, and the diggers run. You heave the stone back into its bed and sit on it, cross-legged, all night. Toward dawn you notice it: the stone rises a little under you, and falls, and rises. Slowly. Like a sleeper. When the sun comes up over the old fortress, the water in the socket is plain rainwater again, and you are not at all sure you have not been sitting on something alive.

events.text: You are at the five-day market on an errand, buying rice. The rice merchant is famous for a heavy thumb and a light measure, and everyone knows it, and everyone buys from him anyway, because his is the only rice. Today his big hanging scale is misbehaving. Every time he leans on it, it reads true. Every time he swaps the weights, it reads true. He is sweating. A queue of grandmothers is watching. And the packed earth of the market square, under your feet, is warm.

choices.text: Buy the scale off him, for the whole market to use

effects.log: You offer him eight taels for the scale, which is twice what it is worth, and he takes it with both hands, glad to be rid of it. You hang it on the old zelkova in the middle of the square for anyone to weigh their rice. It reads true for everyone. The market grows by a third in a year, and the elders give you the first cup at New Year, and the ground under the zelkova is always free of frost.

choices.text: Make him weigh his own weights in front of everyone

effects.log: "Weigh your weights," you say, loud enough for the queue. He has to. The scale reads them true: every one of them light by a tenth. The grandmothers say nothing at all, which is worse than shouting. The merchant goes red, then white, then sells the rest of his rice at a fair price, by noon, and leaves the scale behind him in the dust. Nobody touches it. It hangs there for years, reading true.

choices.text: Crouch down and put your hand on the warm ground

effects.log: You crouch, as if to tie your shoe, and lay your palm flat on the packed earth of the square. It is warm as a stove lid, and under the warm, something huge and patient is paying attention to a rice merchant's scale. You whisper thank you. The warm under your hand rises, a little, the way a cat pushes into a hand. When you stand up, the merchant's scale is reading true, and stays that way.

events.text: You have climbed alone, in the eighteen days before autumn, to the highest peak in the middle of the land to sit and meditate. The four guardians of the directions are in council on a terrace of cloud, and they are quarrelling: the blue banner of the east against the white of the west, the red of the south against the black of the north, over rain and ghosts and songs and slow winters. The centre of their circle is empty. A grey clerk of the council comes to you with a brush behind one ear. "They need something in the middle to face," the clerk says. "You are strong enough to be heard here. Stand in the centre for one season." You step in. At once everything leans on you: every harvest, every war, every king below.

choices.text: Hold it to the last day of the season

ok.log: You hold it. It weighs what the whole world weighs, and you stand in the middle of the quarrel for ninety days with your knees shaking, and the four stop shouting, one by one, to look at you. On the last day the cloud under your feet goes warm, and you feel something vast and patient far below, not yet ready to come up, that has been watching how you carry it. When you step out, you weigh nothing for a month.

fail.log: You hold it, and it nearly breaks you. By the last week your nose bleeds every morning and the clerk brings you a stool, which you refuse. You do not fall. On the last day the cloud under your feet goes warm, as if something far below had put a hand under yours. You come down out of heaven grey-haired at the temples, and proud, and very tired. (-8 health)

choices.text: Set it down halfway, and say so honestly

effects.log: On the forty-fifth day you step out of the centre and say it plainly: "I cannot carry this. It is not mine to carry." The four guardians stop quarrelling to stare. The clerk writes it down. And under the empty centre, very far down, something warm stirs, as if it had been waiting a long time for someone to say exactly that. The season goes on without you. Nothing falls. You learn more from setting it down than from anything you ever lifted.

choices.text: Ask the four who is supposed to be standing here

effects.log: "Who is meant to be here?" you ask the east. The east does not know. You ask the west, the south, the north. You ask every day, for ninety days, until the clerk begs you to stop. On the last day the old Black Tortoise's banner stirs, and a slow voice says: "The yellow one. The centre. It is not born yet." The clerk writes your name on the council's roll, under the empty seat, and underlines it twice.

events.text: Years after your season in the centre, the grey clerk of the council finds you again, brush behind the ear, and bows. "The four would like to know," the clerk says, "what you remember of the weight. They are writing it down for whoever comes next."

choices.text: Say: it is lighter when you share it

effects.log: "It is lighter shared," you say. "That is all I learned." The clerk writes it down, and reads it back, and writes it again more carefully. Years later, you hear, it is the first line of a scroll kept under the empty seat, and nobody is allowed to read the rest until they have read that line.

choices.text: Say: it is heavier than anyone up here thinks

effects.log: "Heavier than any of you think," you say. "Every harvest. Every king." The clerk stops writing and looks up at you with something like respect. "The White Tiger said the same," the clerk says, "and nobody believed it either." They write it down anyway, in red.

events.text: In heaven, word goes round the terraces like wind round a hill: the centre of the guardians' circle has been warm for three days running, though nobody is sitting in it. The grey clerk comes to your door, out of breath, and says the four have asked for you by name.

choices.text: Go, and stand at the edge of the circle

effects.log: You stand at the edge. The four banners stand at the four sides, quiet for once. In the empty middle, the air shimmers gold, like the air over a threshing yard in harvest, and you feel the weight you once held being held by something else, something that can bear it. Nobody says a word. Then the shimmer fades. "Not yet," says the clerk, softly. "But soon."

choices.text: Send word that you will come when the seat is filled

effects.log: You send the clerk back with your answer. A season later the clerk comes again, with a note in a hand nobody recognises, written in what looks like gold dust pressed into yellow clay. It says only: "Thank you for standing where I was not." You keep it in a box. It is always warm.

events.text: You kept a lump of the warm clay from the spade, in a plain white bowl on the shelf. It has never cooled. In the worst cold of the year the family sleeps in a ring round the shelf, and the children say the bowl hums. Now a travelling geomancer has stopped at the gate, sniffed the air, and asked to see what you keep in the house.

choices.text: Show the geomancer the bowl

effects.log: The geomancer looks at the bowl for a long time, very pale, and then walks the whole site with a compass, twice. "Your house is standing on the navel of the valley," the geomancer says. "Something under here has chosen you. Do not dig again in the between-days, and do not sell, and do not ever be cruel in this house." Then the geomancer leaves without asking for a fee, which nobody in the village has ever heard of.

choices.text: Say there is nothing to see

effects.log: "Nothing to see," you say, and shut the gate. The geomancer stands outside a while, then lays a single coin on the gatepost, bows to the house, not to you, and goes on down the road. That winter the bowl on the shelf is warmer than ever, as if pleased with you for keeping it quiet.

events.text: A rich man from the county seat has heard about your house: the house where the rice never runs short, the sick get well, the hens lay in winter. He has come with a sedan chair and a steward and an offer of three times what the house is worth, to buy it, site and all.

choices.text: Refuse, politely

effects.log: You refuse, politely, three times, as manners require. The rich man goes away angry. Within the year his own granary floods, and he comes back with no chair and no steward, and asks, quietly, whether there is anything you would advise. You tell him: be fair to his tenants. He laughs. Then, two years later, you hear he has done it.

choices.text: Ask him why he wants it

effects.log: "Luck," he says. "I want the luck." You hand him the white bowl and let him hold it. In his hands the clay goes cold as a stone, at once. In yours, warm again. He looks at it for a long time, and gives it back, and leaves without a word, and you hear he was kinder to his own household after that.

choices.text: Sell, and take the money

effects.log: You sell. Sixty taels, more money than your family has seen in three generations. You take the white bowl with you; he does not notice. In the new house the clay is cold. By spring it is just clay. In the old house the rich man's rice goes mouldy in the jars, and the hens stop laying, and the walls crack, and in the end nobody lives there at all.

events.text: You are old now, and the house you dug in the forbidden days has outlived three roofs. The youngest of the house has asked why the family never digs in late summer, why the grandmother's grandmother bowed to a bowl, why the yard is warm in snow. You have one evening to tell it.

choices.text: Tell the whole story, the spade and the beat

effects.log: You tell it all: the rain coming, the spade going in, the warm clay that beat like a heart. The child listens with wide eyes. At the end, very solemn, the child goes out into the dark yard and lies down flat and says thank you to the ground. The ground, you are quite sure, says nothing. But in the morning the yard is green in a ring where the child lay.

choices.text: Say only: the ground here was kind to us

effects.log: "The ground here was kind to us," you say, "so we are careful with it." The child nods, disappointed, wanting more. You leave it there. That is how it should be found, you think: not told. Years later, after you are gone, a child of the house will drive a spade in and feel something beat, and know.

events.text: The neighbours have not let you forget the walls you lost to the rain. Now it is late summer again, and the Cho family across the lane are digging a new well in the eighteen days, loud and cheerful, and calling to you over the fence that the old people's taboos are for old people.

choices.text: Go over and ask them to wait

effects.log: You go over and ask, nicely. They laugh. They dig. On the third day the well caves in, with nobody in it, thank heaven, and the water that comes up through the mud is the colour of weak tea and tastes of iron. On the nineteenth day they dig again, a little to the left, quietly, and hit sweet water at once. Mr Cho brings you a jar of it without a word.

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep your own spade in the shed

effects.log: You say nothing. Your own spade stays in the shed until the nineteenth morning. The Cho well caves in twice. When you finally dig your own little vegetable bed, the earth is warm and soft and full of worms, and everything you plant comes up twice the size of anyone else's. The Chos come over to ask how. You shrug.

events.text: A drought year. Every well in the valley has gone down to mud except one: the one in your yard, which you dug on the nineteenth day after the forbidden days, years ago, and which is as full as the day it was dug. There is a queue at your gate with buckets, and it goes round the corner.

choices.text: Let everyone draw, as much as they need

effects.log: You open the gate and let them draw, all day and into the night. The water never goes down. By the end of summer the whole valley calls your well the Patient Well, and the old people use your house as their proof: wait the eighteen days, and the earth repays. You are a little embarrassed. You are also, secretly, very pleased.

choices.text: Share it, but ask each family to keep the taboo next year

effects.log: You share it, and you ask each one, quietly, at the bucket: next late summer, wait the eighteen days. Most of them promise. Next year the valley is oddly quiet at the end of summer, no spades, no new walls, no graves moved. And the year after, the rain comes on time, and every well comes back.

events.text: The tenth month: time to change the rice in the jar you buried at the centre of the house site, the way the shaman said, with the straw cap over it. You lift the cap. The old rice inside is warm, and smells of new straw, and there is more of it than you put in.

choices.text: Make the old rice into cakes for the household only, as the old people say

effects.log: You steam the old rice into cakes and the household eats them, and nobody outside the gate gets a crumb, as the old people say: the luck of the house is not given away. The cakes taste of something you cannot name, like the smell of earth after rain. Nobody in the house is ill that whole winter.

choices.text: Share the cakes with the neighbours anyway

effects.log: You share them over the fence, against all advice. The old people tut. But the next tenth month there is even more rice in the jar than before, and a little of it is the red rice the neighbours grow, and you understand that whatever lives there likes to be talked about over fences.

choices.text: Put the new rice in and say a few words to the jar

effects.log: You pour in the new rice, straighten the straw cap, and say, awkwardly, that you hope the year was a good one down there. The ground under your knees goes warm. Something, very far down and very slowly, seems to turn over in its sleep, contented. You feel foolish and wonderful in equal parts.

events.text: Soldiers of the county are going house to house, taking grain for a war nobody in the valley understands. They have taken the rice from the kitchen, the seed rice from the loft, and now one of them is standing behind the house with a hand on the straw cap of the jar.

choices.text: Stand in front of the jar

ok.log: You stand in front of the jar and do not move. The soldier pushes; you push back, and something under your feet pushes with you, and the soldier sits down hard in the soy-sauce jars. The squad leader looks at the jar, at you, at the ground, and says, "Leave that one." They go. You eat from the jar all winter, a handful a day, and it never runs out.

fail.log: The soldier knocks you down and lifts the cap. The jar is empty: not a grain in it, just dry clay, though you filled it at the tenth month. The soldier swears and goes. When you crawl over and look, it is full again, to the brim, warm rice. You eat from it all winter, a handful a day. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let them look: it is only a spirit jar

effects.log: "Only a spirit jar," you say. "Take it if you like." The soldier lifts the cap. The jar is full of dry yellow clay, nothing else. The soldier spits and goes. That night, when you lift the cap, it is full of warm rice, and you eat from it all winter, a handful a day, and so do the neighbours.

events.text: The first full moon again, and the band is going round. When they reach the old Kim house, the leader stops, and turns, and looks at you. "The Kim yard has not been right since last year," the leader says. "It will not settle for anyone. The grandmother says you have to go first."

choices.text: Go into the yard first, alone, and stamp once

effects.log: You walk into the middle of the yard alone and stamp once. The yard stamps back, once, gently, and the whole band hears it this time: the big drum player drops the stick. Then the yard is still, and settled, and the band plays the best round of the year. The Kim grandmother gives you a whole string of dried persimmons and calls you the little earth-lord.

choices.text: Sit down in the yard and talk to it

effects.log: You sit down cross-legged in the dirt in front of everyone and tell the yard about your year. It takes a while. Somebody laughs; somebody else hushes them. When you get up, the ground where you sat is warm, and the band stamps, and the yard is quiet under them like a sleeping dog. The leader looks at you very strangely all evening.

events.text: You are grown, and the band's old leader has hung up the little gong and handed it to you. This year it is you who leads the ring from yard to yard at the first full moon. At the last house, a new one built on a bare hillside, the ground is cold, cold as a stone in winter, and the family is frightened.

choices.text: Lead the band round three times, stamping

effects.log: You lead them round three times, the gong screaming, everyone stamping. On the third round you feel it: far down, something huge turns its head toward the noise, interested. The cold goes out of the yard like a breath. The family weeps with relief and feeds the whole band until midnight.

choices.text: Send the band home and stamp alone, quietly

effects.log: You send them home and stand in the cold yard alone, and stamp, softly, the way you did as a child. Nothing. Again. Nothing. Then, a long way off, from the direction of the old Kim house, a beat comes back through the ground, as if from a friend across a valley, and the cold yard goes warm under you. You leave without a word.

events.text: The rival sect has not forgotten the night at the sixty-four stones. Three of them are waiting for you on the road home, and their elder wants to know where the relic box is, and what is under the centre stone, and why the crowbars bent.

choices.text: Fight your way through

ok.log: It is a hard fight on a narrow road, and you win it. The elder, on the ground, asks only: "What is under there?" "Something that does not want to be dug up," you say. The rival sect does not come back to the stones. You hear later that their elder gave up the crowbar for a broom, and sweeps a temple yard somewhere in the east.

fail.log: They beat you on the road and search you and find nothing, and leave you in the ditch. At the stones, that night, they dig again. You hear about it later: the ground under the centre stone went soft as rice porridge, and two of them went in up to the waist, and it took all night to get them out. They never came back. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell them the truth: the box weighs what a house weighs

effects.log: You tell them exactly what happened. The elder does not believe a word. Then the youngest of them, who was there that night, says quietly: "It is true. I lifted it. I could not take one step." The elder looks at the youngest a long time, and turns the horses round, and you never see them on that road again.

events.text: A letter, in a shaky hand, from the caretaker of the old temple site: {npc} is dying, has no child, and asks you to come. When you get there, {npc} is lying on a mat beside the centre stone, under the open sky, and the rainwater in the socket is gold.

choices.text: Promise to keep the stones

effects.log: You promise. {npc} smiles and puts your hand flat on the centre stone. It is warm, and it rises, very slowly, under your palm, and falls. "It breathes," {npc} whispers. "Six hundred years and nobody believed me." {npc} dies at dawn. You come back every late summer after that, and pull the weeds from round the sixty-four stones, and sit on the centre one until the sun goes down.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what is really under the stone

effects.log: "The temple was built on a marsh," {npc} says, "where a king meant to build a palace, until a yellow dragon came up out of the mud. The king built a temple instead, and a pagoda nine storeys high, and the dragon stayed under it, holding it up. The horsemen burned it. The dragon stayed anyway." {npc} closes both eyes. "I think it is waiting for the pagoda to come back. I think it will wait for ever."

events.text: The county's new tax officer has come to the five-day market with the official grain measures, and they are, everyone can see, a good fifth too big. The farmers are being taxed a fifth over. Somebody in the crowd shouts that the old scale in the square reads true, and the officer should try it.

choices.text: Carry the officer's measures to the scale

effects.log: You carry the measures to the scale in front of the whole market. The scale reads them: a fifth over, every one. The officer goes the colour of a boiled crab. That evening the magistrate himself comes to see, and weighs, and goes away very thoughtful, and the measures are recut by the next market day. You did not know a market could cheer like that.

choices.text: Talk to the officer quietly, before it becomes a riot

effects.log: You take the officer aside. "They will riot," you say, "and you will be blamed, not whoever cut the measures." The officer, who is young and frightened, weighs the measures on the scale in private. A fifth over. The officer goes white, and takes the fifth off by hand, all day, with you holding the sacks, and writes a report that gets a much older official dismissed.

events.text: The scale in the square has been stolen in the night. The whole market is in mourning. Then a child comes running: there is a rich merchant's wagon stuck on the county road, its wheels sunk to the axles in the dry, hard earth, and the scale is in the back of it.

choices.text: Go and get it back

ok.log: The guards fight; the earth under them keeps tilting, very slightly, toward you. You carry the scale back to the market on your shoulder with half the town walking behind. The merchant's wagon stays stuck until he walks to the market himself and apologises in front of everyone. Then it rolls out as if on ice.

fail.log: The guards knock you flat. But as they drive off, the earth simply opens under the back wheels, softly, like a mouth, and the scale slides out of the wagon and onto the road, and the ground closes. You carry it back, bruised. Nobody steals it again. (-7 health)

choices.text: Wait: let the ground decide

effects.log: "Wait," you tell the market. By evening the merchant has tried oxen, levers and prayer, and the wagon is deeper than ever. At sunset he gets out, lifts the scale off the wagon, and sets it on the road. The wagon rolls free. He drives off without it, and the children carry it home singing.

events.text: The richest family in the valley wants to move their grandfather's grave to a better hillside a geomancer has found for them, and they want it done now, in the eighteen days before autumn, because the geomancer says the new site will not wait. They are hiring every strong back in the valley. The pay is good. The old people are muttering.

choices.text: Take the work: the pay is good

effects.log: You take the work. The first spade into the old mound comes up full of yellow clay, warm, and the second, and the third, and by noon nobody will say a word, and the whole hillside feels as if it were holding its breath. The coffin comes out. The new grave goes in. That night every dog in the valley howls until dawn. You keep the six taels in a jar and do not spend them for a long time.

choices.text: Refuse, and say why

effects.log: You refuse, to the steward's face, and say why: the earth belongs to itself in the between-days. The steward laughs and hires someone else. But three other young people in the valley refuse too, because you did, and the old people look at you differently after that, as if you had said something they had stopped expecting to hear.

choices.text: Go to the head of the family and ask them to wait the eighteen days

ok.log: You talk for an hour on the family's veranda. In the end the head of the family, an old man tired of being told what to do by geomancers, sends the diggers home. "Nineteen days," the old man says. "If the site has gone, so be it." The site has not gone. The grandfather is moved on the nineteenth day, in sunshine, and the earth comes up cool and quiet and ordinary.

fail.log: You talk for an hour and get nowhere. The steward has you shown out. The grave is moved in the forbidden days, and that autumn the rich family's rice rots in the barns, and the geomancer leaves the county by night. Nobody says you were right. Everybody looks at you as if you were.

events.text: Late summer again, and in the night you dream of the moved grave. In the dream the hillside is a sleeper's back, and the opened mound is a wound, and something under it is waiting, very patiently, to be put right. You wake with yellow dust on your pillow.

choices.text: Go up the hill with rice and water and say sorry

effects.log: You climb the hillside at dawn with a bowl of rice and a bowl of water and set them on the scar of the old mound, and say sorry, for all of you. The ground is cold. Then, under your knees, it goes warm, slowly, the way a hand warms in yours. Grass grows over the scar that autumn, thick and green. Nobody else in the valley mentions it.

choices.text: Ask the old people what they know about the between-days

effects.log: The oldest grandmother in the valley tells you, over a long afternoon: each season belongs to one of the four, wood and fire and metal and water, and the last eighteen days before each new season belong to the centre, to earth, which has no season of its own because it holds them all together. "You do not dig into someone's hands while they are passing you a bowl," she says. It is the clearest thing anyone has ever told you.

events.text: You are old enough now that the young people of the valley come to you about the taboos. A young couple want to raise their house in the eighteen days, because the timber is cut and the carpenter is free and the rain is coming. They are asking your leave, the way you once heard the old people asked.

choices.text: Tell them to wait, and help them keep the timber dry

effects.log: You tell them to wait, and then you spend the next eighteen days with them, roping straw over the stacked timber every time it rains. On the nineteenth morning the posts go in, and the earth under the site is warm and willing, and the house goes up in a week. They name their first child after you, a little, in the middle.

choices.text: Tell them to bury a jar of rice at the centre first, and then build

effects.log: "Put a roof over whatever lives there," you say, "before you put one over yourselves." They bury a small jar of new rice with a straw cap at the centre of the site. The earth sighs, or the wind does. The house goes up in the forbidden days, and nothing goes wrong, and they keep the jar for years.

events.text: You have been given the night watch at the crossroads outside the village, where five roads meet under the old spirit poles. It is the dullest duty there is. And every single night, around the hour of the rat, you fall asleep sitting up, warm as a child on a heated floor, however cold the wind, however hard you pinch yourself.

choices.text: Stay awake by walking the roads all night

effects.log: You walk the five roads all night, up and back, up and back. You stay awake. And you notice, walking, that the roads are warm, all five, from the crossroads out to about a hundred paces, and then cold. Something under the crossroads is warm, and big, and the roads run over it like ribbons over a sleeping back.

choices.text: Let yourself sleep, and see what happens

effects.log: You let yourself sleep. You wake at dawn rested and warm, spear still across your knees. In the dust around you are tracks: a fox's, coming up to the edge of the crossroads and turning back, and a wild boar's, the same, and a man's, the same. Nothing crossed the middle. Nothing has crossed the middle all year, you realise, while you slept.

events.text: A band of horse thieves comes through on the north road at midnight, quiet, lanterns hooded. You are asleep at your post, as usual. You wake with a start: the ground under you has given one hard shove, like a bed being kicked.

choices.text: Raise the alarm and hold the crossroads

ok.log: You bang the gong and stand in the middle of the crossroads with your spear, and the thieves' horses will not cross it: they shy, every one, at the middle, as if at a snake. The village comes running. The thieves scatter. In the morning the headman praises you for being wide awake. You do not correct the headman.

fail.log: You bang the gong and one of the thieves rides you down. But their horses will not cross the middle of the crossroads, not for whip or spur, and by the time they go round through the paddies the village is up. You get a broken rib and a reputation. (-6 health)

choices.text: Lie still and let the ground deal with it

effects.log: You lie still. The thieves come to the crossroads, and their horses stop dead at the middle, and rear, and turn, and will not go on, and the thieves sit there in the dark arguing, until the dogs in the village wake up and they have to go back the way they came. You are, technically, the hero. You feel, technically, like a fraud.

events.text: Years later, passing through your old village, you stop at the crossroads. A new young watchman is asleep against the spirit pole, spear across the knees, mouth open. The headman's grandchild, now the headman, is marching up to wake the poor creature with a stick.

choices.text: Stop the headman: let the watch sleep

effects.log: "Let them sleep," you say. "It is the best-guarded crossroads in the county." You tell the headman why, at length, over tea. The headman laughs, and then stops laughing, and in the end decides the watch at the crossroads will be a post of honour from now on, and nobody will be beaten for sleeping on it.

choices.text: Sit down beside the sleeping watch, and keep it company

effects.log: You sit down by the spirit pole beside the sleeping youngster and put your palm on the dirt. Warm. Warmer than you remember. Whatever is down there has grown. You sit till dawn. The youngster wakes and finds a stranger beside them, and you just say: "Good watch," and walk on.

events.text: On the road between markets you fall in with {npc}, a pack-peddler with a wooden carrier heaped higher than {his} head. At every crossroads {npc} stops, sets down the carrier, adds a stone to the cairn, and bows. "For luck," {npc} says. "I have walked these roads forty years and the crossroads have never once let me down."

choices.text: Bow at the next crossroads too

effects.log: At the next crossroads you add a stone and bow beside {npc}. The dust under your feet is warm, the way a seat is warm when someone has only just stood up. {npc} grins. "You felt it," {npc} says. "Most people do not. Walk with me to the next market, and I will show you which roads are friendly."

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the crossroads has ever done for anybody

effects.log: "Done?" {npc} laughs. "Bandits on the west road, every year, and they never once found me. Floods on the south road, and I was always a day ahead. A crossroads is where things meet. Something sits there and sorts them out. I say thank you. That is all." You walk on together, and you notice you are counting the crossroads.

events.text: {npc} the peddler is in trouble: a market lord has told every stall-keeper in the county not to buy from {him}, because {npc} sells needles and salt at a fair price and the market lord's own people do not. {npc} has come to you, carrier and all, very tired.

choices.text: Walk {npc} to the market lord and stand behind {him}

ok.log: The market lord's strongmen try to turn you both away at the gate. They fail. You stand behind {npc} while {npc} lays out needles and salt on a straw mat in the middle of the square, at the old fair price, and the stall-keepers, one by one, come to buy. The market lord sulks for a year and then lowers the prices at every stall the lord owns.

fail.log: The strongmen throw you both in the ditch. {npc} sits up, brushes off the salt, and says: "Next crossroads." At the next crossroads, {npc} bows. Three markets later the market lord's warehouse floods in a dry spell, water coming up through the floor, and {npc} is back in business. (-7 health)

choices.text: Help {npc} find a new round of markets on the far roads

effects.log: You spend a season walking new roads with {npc}, bowing at every crossroads, and every one of them is warm, and leads somewhere good. By winter {npc} has a better round than before, through hill villages that never see a peddler, where the grandmothers wait at the gate. "See," {npc} says. "Never once let me down."

events.text: Word comes that {npc} the peddler has died on the road, at a crossroads, sitting with {his} back against the cairn, carrier beside {him}, as if resting. The village nearby does not know who {npc} was, and is about to bury the stranger in the paupers' field.

choices.text: Go, and bury {npc} at the crossroads

effects.npcPass: old age, on the road, at a crossroads
effects.log: You go, and you pay, and you bury {npc} beside the cairn at the crossroads, where five roads meet, with the carrier. When the first spade goes in the earth is warm and soft as bread. You put a stone on the cairn and bow. Years later travellers say it is the luckiest crossroads in the county, and nobody knows why.

choices.text: Finish {npc}'s last round of markets, with the carrier

effects.npcPass: old age, on the road, at a crossroads
effects.log: You take up {npc}'s carrier and walk the last round of markets, every one, bowing at every crossroads, and at every market a grandmother asks where the old peddler is, and you tell them. At the last crossroads the dust is warm, and a gust of wind lifts and sets down, like someone shifting a load from one shoulder to the other. You leave the carrier there.

events.text: You have been hired as a bodyguard to {npc}, the young heir of a mountain lord, famous for being far too strong. A neighbouring lord, who rules a little hill country that calls itself the Kingdom of the Yellow Dragon, has sent {npc} a gift: a great horn bow, to test {him}. {npc} picks it up, smiles, and bends it until it snaps.
events.arc: The Bow and the Yellow Dragon

choices.text: Tell {npc} that was a mistake

effects.log: "That was meant as a test," you say, "and you have just told a neighbour you are dangerous." {npc} laughs it off. But the next month a letter comes from {npc}'s own father, the mountain lord, to the neighbouring lord, and you happen to see it sealed, and you have a bad feeling about it.

choices.text: Say nothing; it was a fine piece of strength

effects.log: You say nothing. It was, in fact, magnificent. {npc} is proud and pleased all week. Then a letter goes from {npc}'s father to the neighbouring lord, sealed with black wax, and the household goes quiet in a way you do not like at all.

events.text: {npc} has been invited to the hill country of the Yellow Dragon as a guest, and you go along as guard. You know what the black-sealed letter said: the father asked the neighbour to kill {npc}, an heir too strong to be safe. In the feasting hall the neighbouring lord rises, sword at the hip, and looks at {npc} for a long time.
events.arc: The Bow and the Yellow Dragon

choices.text: Stand between them

roll.foeName: The lord of the Yellow Dragon hills

ok.log: You step between them, hand on your hilt. The lord's sword does not come out. The lord looks past you at {npc}, young and strong and laughing at the feast, and you see the lord's face change. "I cannot do it," the lord says, quietly, to nobody. "Not to a guest." {npc} goes home loaded with gifts and never knows. Under the hall, the floor is warm all night.

fail.log: You step between them and the lord's guards put you on the floor before you can draw. But the lord's sword stays in its sheath. The lord stands over {npc} a long time, and then says: "I cannot. Not a guest under my roof." You go home bruised, with {npc} loaded with gifts. You do not tell {npc} anything. (-8 health)

choices.text: Watch the lord's face, and wait

effects.log: You wait, very still. The lord's hand is on the hilt. Then the lord looks at {npc}, really looks, and the hand comes away. "Guests are sacred in these hills," the lord says to the hall. "We are named for the centre. The centre does not murder what comes to it." {npc} is sent home with courtesy and gifts, and never learns how close it was.

events.text: {npc} has come into the lordship at last, and it has not gone well: too strong, too proud, quarrelling with every elder. {npc} has asked you to come and talk, the only one who was there in the hall of the Yellow Dragon hills.
events.arc: The Bow and the Yellow Dragon

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth about the black-sealed letter

effects.log: You tell {npc} everything: the letter, the sword, the lord who could not. {npc} sits very still for a long time. Then {npc} goes out and sends a gift to the hill country, and then, slower, to every elder {npc} has quarrelled with. It is the first gentle thing anyone has seen {npc} do. It is not the last.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the hill lord's words: the centre does not murder what comes to it

effects.log: You give {npc} the words, nothing else. {npc} turns them over for days. At the next council, when a hothead elder says something unforgivable, {npc} pours the elder a cup of wine instead of drawing. The elders talk about it for a year. The hill country, you hear, has a warm winter.

events.text: Harvest, and the whole family is out on the threshing yard with flails, beating the rice off the straw. You stop to wipe your face, look down, and see under the thin dust of the yard two great round shapes, gold, the size of millstones, very faintly glowing. They blink.

choices.text: Keep threshing, and say nothing

effects.log: You keep threshing. The eyes watch the flails rise and fall all afternoon, contentedly, the way an old dog watches the family at work. The rice comes off the straw cleaner than any year you remember. At sunset, the eyes close. That night you sleep like a stone.

choices.text: Sweep the dust off for a better look

effects.log: You sweep. Under the dust there is only packed yellow earth, hard and warm, warmer than the sun could make it. No eyes. But the broom tingles in your hands, and the old woman beside you, has seen your face and is looking at the yard very carefully indeed.

choices.text: Shout for the family to come and look

effects.log: The whole family comes running and stares at the yard. Nothing. Dust. They laugh at you for the rest of the harvest. But the grandmother, after supper, takes a bowl of the new rice out to the middle of the yard and leaves it there, and in the morning it is gone, and she does not laugh.

events.text: A bad year. The harvest is thin and the landlord's steward has come to the threshing yard to take the rent, with a measure that everyone knows is too big. The family stands round the little pile of rice in silence. Under the dust, if you look, the two gold shapes are open.

choices.text: Ask the steward to measure on the yard itself

effects.log: "Measure here," you say, "on the yard." The steward shrugs and scoops. The measure comes up a fifth short every time, however it is heaped, as if the rice were slipping out the bottom. The steward tries for an hour, sweating, and in the end takes what the measure holds and goes. The family eats that winter.

choices.text: Stand in front of the rice

ok.log: You stand in front of the rice and refuse. The steward shoves; you do not move; the yard under you does not move either, and the steward ends up sitting in the chaff. The steward takes a fair measure and leaves in a temper. The landlord never sends that steward again.

fail.log: The steward's men knock you down. They take the rent with the big measure. And then, crossing the yard with the sacks, they sink to their ankles in the hard-packed earth, every step, as if wading, and by the gate they have spilled half the sacks into the dust. You and the family sweep it up after dark. (-6 health)

events.text: The old threshing yard of your family is going to be sold off for a new road. The surveyors are already there with their poles. You go and stand on it one last time at harvest. The dust is thin. Nothing glows.

choices.text: Kneel and say goodbye

effects.log: You kneel and put both hands flat on the yard and say goodbye, and thank you, for every harvest. For a moment there is nothing. Then the yard warms under your hands, and two faint gold shapes open under the dust, and look at you, and close. The road goes through the next spring. Travellers say the stretch over the old yard is the only part that never floods.

choices.text: Go to the county office and ask for the road to go round

ok.log: You make such a nuisance of yourself at the county office that the clerk, to get rid of you, redraws the line. The road bends round the old yard in a great unnecessary curve that every carter curses. The yard stays. Children play on it at harvest. On warm evenings it is warmer.

fail.log: The clerk does not redraw the line. The road goes through. But the builders cannot get the road to set over the old yard: it cracks, every spring, in two round rings, and they patch it, and it cracks. In the end they leave the rings as they are, and carters steer round them, for luck.

events.text: At the village rite the shaman holds out five furled flags, blue, red, white, black and yellow, and tells you to pick one, without looking, to learn your year: blue for luck in work, red for good fortune, white for mourning, black for danger, yellow for... the shaman hesitates. "Yellow is the centre. Nobody draws yellow."

choices.text: Pick, without looking

ok.log: You pull a flag and unfurl it. Yellow. The drums stop. The shaman looks at it, and at you, and kneels, very slowly, in front of the whole village, and touches forehead to the ground. "The centre has looked at you," the shaman says afterwards, quietly. "Everything will lean on you this year. Lean back on the ground."

fail.log: You pull a flag and unfurl it. Blue: luck in work. The crowd claps. But as you hand it back, the yellow flag in the shaman's other hand comes unfurled by itself, in no wind, and hangs there, and the shaman looks at it, and at you, and goes very quiet.

choices.text: Ask why nobody draws yellow

effects.log: "Because yellow is not a year," the shaman says, after the rite, over cold rice wine. "Blue is spring, red summer, white autumn, black winter. Yellow is the middle of all of them. It holds them together and has no season of its own. If you drew yellow, the year would not be yours. You would be the year's." You think about that for a long time.

events.text: Everything has leaned on you this year, as if the yellow flag had meant it: a sick parent in the house next door, a neighbour's lawsuit, a flooded field that is not even yours, three quarrels brought to you to settle. You are worn thin. Tonight you lie down on the bare earth of the yard because the floor is too hot to sleep on.

choices.text: Lean back on the ground

effects.log: You lie on your back on the yard and let it all go into the earth, the parent, the lawsuit, the flood, the quarrels, one at a time. The ground takes them, warm and patient and immense, and does not seem to mind. You sleep there till dawn. In the morning everything is still there to be done, but none of it is heavy any more. (+8 health)

choices.text: Get up and finish the work

effects.log: You get up. You finish the work: the parent nursed, the lawsuit settled, the field drained, the quarrels mended, by the end of autumn. You are exhausted and proud. And on the last night, lying on the yard, you notice the ground has been warm under you all year, every night, the whole time, holding you up.

events.text: A famine winter. The county granary is sealed by order of the magistrate, who is away in the capital, and the clerk will not open it without the seal. The village is eating bark. The clerk has given you the key to guard, because you are the only one strong enough to keep the crowd off the door. Under the granary floor, through the cracks, comes a faint gold light.

choices.text: Open the granary and give out the rice

effects.log: You open it. The crowd is silent, then weeping. You give out rice by the measure, fairly, all night. In the morning the granary seems as full as when you began; the clerk counts it twice and goes pale. When the magistrate comes home, the books balance to the grain, and there is nothing at all to punish you for.

choices.text: Keep the door shut, as ordered, and send a runner to the magistrate

effects.log: You keep the door shut and send the fastest runner in the village. It is the longest ten days of your life. On the tenth night the gold light under the granary goes out, and in the morning the door is found standing open, lock unbroken, and rice spilled down the steps for anyone to take. Nobody saw who. The runner comes back with the seal on the eleventh day.

events.text: The magistrate is home from the capital and has called you to the yamen about the granary. The magistrate is furious, or is pretending to be, and keeps glancing at the floor, as if something under it were listening.

choices.text: Tell the magistrate exactly what happened

effects.log: You tell it straight. The magistrate listens, and then says, unexpectedly: "The floor of this yamen gets heavy when I am unjust. Did you know that? Like sitting on a sack of wet rice." The magistrate dismisses you with no punishment, and that spring sets up a famine store in every village, with the key kept by an elder.

choices.text: Say the granary opened itself

effects.log: "It opened itself," you say, and you can see the magistrate decide to believe you, and be relieved. "Then the centre of the county has spoken," the magistrate says, "and I have nothing to add." You are sent home with a bag of rice for your trouble, and that spring the villages quietly start famine stores of their own, with the key kept by an elder.

events.text: {npc}, captain of the county guard, has asked you to drink with {him} after your errand at the yamen. Halfway down the jar {npc} leans in and asks a strange question: "Whose county is this, really? Not the magistrate's. The magistrates come and go. Something here outlasts them. When a bad one sits in that hall, the whole yard groans."

choices.text: Say: it belongs to the ground it stands on

effects.log: "To the ground," you say. {npc} stares at you, then laughs, then stops laughing. "Yes," {npc} says. "Come with me." In the empty yamen courtyard at midnight {npc} kneels and lays a palm on the paving. You do the same. Warm. And heavy, somehow, as if the stones were pressing up. "Six magistrates," {npc} says. "I can tell you which ones were cruel by how the yard felt."

choices.text: Say: to the people who live in it

effects.log: "To the people in it," you say. {npc} nods slowly. "And the people," {npc} says, "stand on something." Later, walking you to the gate, {npc} stops in the courtyard and stamps, once, and the paving gives back a deep, slow sound, like a drum heard through a wall. "There," {npc} says. "That is who I mean."

events.text: {npc} the captain sends for you in a hurry. The new magistrate is the worst the county has had in living memory: taxes doubled, a widow's land taken, a clerk flogged for honesty. And the yamen courtyard has begun to crack, in a great ring round the magistrate's hall, wider every day.

choices.text: Go and gather proof for the provincial inspector

effects.log: You and {npc} spend a month gathering it: the doubled tax rolls, the widow's deed, the flogged clerk's testimony. The provincial inspector comes in disguise, reads it in an inn, and walks into the yamen the next morning with the seal of office. The magistrate is taken away in a cart. That night the ring in the courtyard closes up like a healing cut.

choices.text: Stand guard over the widow's land with {npc}

ok.log: You and {npc} stand at the widow's boundary stones when the magistrate's runners come with ropes. They do not get past. A week later the magistrate, crossing the cracked courtyard, falls through the paving to the waist and is pulled out by the guard, white and silent, and resigns the seal before the month is out.

fail.log: The runners beat you both and rope the boundary stones. But the next morning the stones are back in place, upright, rooted deep as old trees, and nobody can move them, and the magistrate, crossing the courtyard, falls through the cracking paving and resigns the seal. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc} the old captain is retiring, and has asked you to the yamen courtyard for the last night watch together. A good magistrate sits in the hall now. The courtyard is quiet. {npc} sits down on the paving and pats the place beside {him}.

choices.text: Sit, and keep the watch in silence

effects.log: You sit together on the warm stones all night and say almost nothing. Near dawn {npc} says: "I always wondered if it knew I was here." Under you the paving rises, very slightly, and falls, like a sleeper turning toward someone in bed. {npc} laughs softly, and wipes both eyes, and goes home.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what forty years of guarding it taught

effects.log: "That the hall is not the centre," {npc} says. "The ground is. The hall only sits on it. A good magistrate knows the difference." {npc} gives you a short wooden baton worn smooth by forty years of hands. You keep it. Whenever you hold it, your feet feel heavy and rooted, and you think more slowly, and better.

events.text: A magistrate has hired you, quietly, for a great deal of money. "There is something under my hall," {npc} says. "Every time I sign a judgement, the brush gets heavy. Some days I cannot lift it. Some days I cannot get out of the chair. Find it and get rid of it." On the desk, under a cloth, is a stack of silver that did not come from the magistrate's salary.

choices.text: Take the job, and look under the floor

effects.log: You take the twenty taels and lift the floorboards. Under the hall there is only earth: packed, yellow, and warm as a living back, and when you put your hand on it you feel the weight the magistrate means. It is not the brush that is heavy. It is the judgements. You put the boards back and go to think.

choices.text: Ask {npc} which judgements were heavy

effects.log: {npc} does not want to say, then says. The land case the rich family won. The tax remission refused. The thief from the hills hanged on thin evidence. The pardon for the steward's nephew. You do not need to look under the floor at all. You tell {npc} so. {npc} goes very red and says you may keep the advance.

choices.text: Refuse: you know what is heavy

effects.log: "It is not under the floor," you say. "It is on the desk," and you nod at the silver, and walk out. Behind you there is a long silence, and then a creak, as if the magistrate had sat down very heavily, and could not get up.

events.text: {npc} the magistrate has hired a sect of diggers from the capital to dig out whatever is under the hall, since you would not. They have been at it three days. The deeper they go, the warmer the earth, and the hall above is leaning, and the whole county is holding its breath.

choices.text: Stop the diggers before the hall falls

ok.log: You drop into the pit and the foreman meets you with a pick handle. It is a hard fight in a hot hole. You win it, and the diggers climb out, and the hall eases back upright with a groan of timber. {npc} stands at the edge of the pit, shaking, looking down at the warm yellow earth as if seeing it for the first time.

fail.log: The foreman lays you out in the pit. You lie in the warm yellow earth with the diggers' picks going in all round you, and then the earth simply rises, a hand's breadth, everywhere at once, like a chest breathing in, and the diggers drop their picks and run, and the hall rights itself. {npc} hauls you out by the collar. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go to {npc} and say: undo the heavy judgements

effects.log: You go up to the hall and lay it out for {npc}: undo the land case, grant the remission, free the hills thief's family, revoke the pardon. {npc} argues for an hour. Then {npc} tries lifting the brush, and it will not lift. {npc} begins to write the reversals. With each one the brush gets lighter. The diggers are sent home before dark.

events.text: {npc} the magistrate, now retired and quite poor, writes to you from a little house in the hills. "I still sign my letters," {npc} writes, "and the brush is light. I wanted someone to know. Come and eat with me, if you will."

choices.text: Go and eat with {npc}

effects.log: You go. The house is small, the rice is plain, the yard is warm. {npc} shows you a ledger: every heavy judgement {npc} ever signed, and beside each one what was done to set it right. It took twenty years. "The last one," {npc} says, "I finished this spring. I have never slept so well."

choices.text: Send rice and a letter instead

effects.log: You send a sack of good rice and a letter. {npc} writes back: "The rice was good. The letter was better. Under this little house there is nothing at all, just ordinary earth, and I am so glad." You laugh out loud reading it, alone, and do not know why your eyes sting.

events.text: The master of a rising sect has asked you, as a guest of rank, to witness the founding of the new sect hall. The site is a round green knoll in the exact middle of the valley, which every geomancer for fifty li calls the navel of the land. The old village geomancer is standing in front of the builders, refusing to move.

choices.text: Back the geomancer: some places are not for building

effects.log: You stand beside the old geomancer. The sect master is furious, and then, seeing you will not move, thoughtful. "Then where?" the master asks. "To one side," says the geomancer, "facing it. A house that sits beside the centre is lucky. A house that sits on it is crushed." The hall is built at the foot of the knoll, facing it. It prospers.

choices.text: Let them build: it is not your valley

effects.log: You stand back. The builders dig. The earth of the knoll is warm and dense as clay in a kiln, and every post they sink rises again overnight, an inch, two inches, pushed up from below. By the end of the month the hall is still only posts, and the posts lean outward like a flower opening, and the sect master sends for you.

choices.text: Walk up onto the knoll and stand on it first

effects.log: You walk up the knoll, before anyone can stop you, and stand on the very top. It is like standing on the crown of a great sleeping head. Everything in the valley leans toward you: the rivers, the roads, the fields, the wind. You come down quickly, dizzy. "Not there," you tell the master. The master, who saw your face, does not argue.

events.text: The sect at the foot of the knoll has grown great, and its master, now old, has begun to want the knoll after all: a pavilion on the top, just a small one, for meditation. The disciples are hauling timber up the slope. Under the grass, the knoll is warm as a hearthstone.

choices.text: Climb up and talk the old master out of it

ok.log: You sit with the old master on the slope all afternoon. "You have spent your whole life prospering beside the centre," you say. "Do not spend the end of it trying to sit on it." The old master laughs, a long creaky laugh, and sends the timber back down. They build the pavilion at the foot of the knoll instead, facing it, and it is the best place in the valley to sit.

fail.log: The old master will not hear it. The pavilion goes up on the top of the knoll. That winter, without a sound, the knoll turns over in its sleep, and the pavilion slides gently down the slope in one piece and settles at the bottom, facing it, undamaged, the tea still warm in the cups. Nobody tries again.

choices.text: Leave it: the knoll can look after itself

effects.log: You leave it. The disciples carry the timber up all week. Every morning they find it carried back down again and stacked neatly at the foot of the knoll. By the eighth day the old master comes out to watch, and laughs, and says, "Very well, very well," to the knoll, and the timber stays where it is put, at the bottom.

events.text: The king of the old kingdom is raising a wooden pagoda nine storeys high, and has hired a master builder from an enemy kingdom, the best alive, with two hundred craftsmen. You are hired to keep order on the site. Today they raise the centre pillar, a whole great tree, the height of a hill. Halfway up, the earth shakes, and the sky goes dark at noon, and the ropes begin to slip.

choices.text: Throw your strength onto the ropes

ok.log: You take a rope and pull with everything you have. It is not enough; nothing would be enough. And then there are two more at the foot of the pillar who were not there before: an old monk in a patched robe and a broad strong man in plain clothes, who put their hands on the great tree and lift it, simply lift it, upright, into its socket, as if it were a broom. The earth goes still. The sky clears. When you look round, they are gone.

fail.log: You take a rope and it burns through your hands and drags you across the site. Lying in the dirt you see two figures who were not there before, an old monk and a broad strong man, put their hands on the falling pillar and lift it upright into its socket. The earth goes still. Nobody knows where they went. You have rope scars on both palms for life. (-8 health)

choices.text: Run to the master builder: something is wrong

effects.log: You run to the master builder, who is on the scaffold staring at nothing, grey in the face. "I dreamed my own kingdom falling," the builder whispers. "Just now. Awake." Below, two strangers, an old monk and a strong man, have their hands on the pillar, and it is rising, upright, into its socket, and the earth goes still. The builder sits down on the scaffold and weeps.

events.text: Before the pillar is sealed, the abbot lays a box of relics, a hundred of them, in the hollow under it. The whole site kneels. As the box goes into the dark, you feel the ground under your knees take the weight of it, and of the pillar, and of the nine storeys still to come, and settle, the way a bearer settles a load.

choices.text: Bow to the ground, not the relics

effects.log: You bow to the ground. An old monk next to you, patched robe, a face you half remember, sees it and smiles. "Good," the monk says. "Everyone bows to the box. The box does not hold anything up." When you look again the monk is gone, and where the monk knelt there is a print in the earth, warm.

choices.text: Look for the old monk and the strong man

effects.log: You look for them all through the ceremony. Nobody has seen them; nobody else even remembers them. That night you walk the site alone. At the foot of the pillar, in the fresh earth, there are two sets of footprints, an old monk's sandals and a big bare foot, going down into the ground, not away. You do not tell anyone.

events.text: The pagoda is finished, nine storeys of red-lacquered wood, the tallest thing in the world, and they say nine nations will bow to the kingdom because of it. On the night of the dedication lightning strikes the top storey. The whole capital sees it. The pagoda does not burn.

choices.text: Climb to the top and see the damage

effects.log: You climb in the rain, nine storeys, and at the top the lightning has left a black scar on the finial, nothing more. From there you can see the whole capital, and you notice, looking down, that the pagoda's shadow under the moon is not a pagoda's shadow. It is long, and coiled, and has a head. You climb down very carefully.

choices.text: Go down to the foot of the pillar and put a hand on it

effects.log: You go down into the dark at the foot of the centre pillar and lay your hand on it. It is warm, and it trembles, very faintly, the way a strong arm trembles holding something heavy for a long time. "Thank you," you say. The trembling eases. You come back to the pillar every year after, while you live in the capital.

events.text: {npc}, the master builder of the pagoda, is from the enemy kingdom to the west, and has been paid in gold to raise a tower meant to make that same kingdom bow. You find {npc} at night on the scaffold, looking west. "I dreamed my home falling," {npc} says. "Every night since the pillar. Should I stop?"

choices.text: Say: finish it, and build it true

effects.log: "Finish it," you say. "A builder who builds badly to hurt an enemy is not a builder." {npc} is silent a long time. "The ground here would not let me build badly anyway," {npc} says at last. "Every crooked joint I make, I find straight in the morning." The work goes on, and it is the best work of {npc}'s life.

choices.text: Say: go home

effects.log: "Go home," you say. "Nobody should build the fall of their own country." {npc} packs a bag that night. In the morning {npc} is still there, on the scaffold, working. "I tried," {npc} says. "The road west was a mud wallow up to the knees, in a dry month. I think I am meant to finish it."

events.text: News from the west: the enemy kingdom has fallen, as {npc} dreamed. {npc} the builder has no home to go back to. The pagoda is finished. The king has offered {npc} a house in the capital, and a title, and {npc} has asked you to come and help decide.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to stay, and build for the living

effects.log: "Stay," you say, "and build bridges, and granaries, and schools." {npc} stays. For years {npc} builds things that hold people up instead of making them bow. When {npc} dies they bury {npc} near the pagoda, and the earth there is warm in winter.

choices.text: Help {npc} go west and build on the ruins

effects.log: You ride west with {npc} to the ruined capital of the fallen kingdom. {npc} walks the ashes for a week, and then begins, with a few survivors, to build a small temple on the old palace site. It is nothing like the pagoda. It stands for six hundred years.

events.text: A courtier has offered you a fortune to swear, before the chroniclers, that you saw a yellow dragon rise over the king's new hunting lodge. Yellow dragons, everyone knows, appear when a dynasty is blessed. The king is unpopular. A sighting, written into the annals, would help. "Nobody gets hurt," the courtier says.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: You refuse. The courtier finds someone else. The annals record a yellow dragon over the hunting lodge. Within the year the lodge's wells go dry and its foundations crack, and the courtier is quietly sent to a far province. You hear an old chronicler say, on a terrace: "It does not like being lied about."

choices.text: Take the money and swear

effects.log: You swear it and take thirty taels. The annals record your words. That night, and every night for a month, you dream of a great golden eye opening under your bed, looking at you without anger, only with patience, as if waiting for you to say something else.

choices.text: Go to the chroniclers yourself and tell them about the offer

ok.log: You tell the oldest chronicler everything. The old chronicler listens, then writes in the annals, in tiny characters: "This year a courtier paid for a dragon. None came." The courtier is ruined. The chroniclers send you a jar of good wine every New Year after.

fail.log: The chronicler hears you out and says, tiredly, that the annals have recorded eleven paid dragons this reign. Nobody will act. But the chronicler writes your name down anyway, in the margin, with the word "refused", and you feel oddly as if something heard it.

events.text: Something has been seen. Over the barley fields east of the capital, at dawn, by forty farmers at once: a great golden shape in the clouds, coiled, looking down. No courtier paid for it. The whole capital is in uproar, and the chroniclers have sent for you, as the one person in the city known to have refused to lie about dragons.

choices.text: Go to the fields and speak to the farmers

effects.log: You walk the fields for three days and talk to all forty. Their stories agree in the small things, which liars never manage: the smell of wet clay, the warm wind out of the east, the way the barley all bowed the same way at once. You tell the chroniclers: it was real. The annals record it in plain words. That year a good heir is born to the royal house.

choices.text: Tell the chroniclers to write only what was seen

effects.log: "Write what was seen," you say. "Not what it means." They write: "Forty farmers saw a golden shape over the barley at dawn." Nothing about blessings or dynasties. Years later a scholar calls it the most honest entry in the annals of the reign, and you are rather proud of it.

events.text: You lied about a dragon once, for thirty taels, and the annals still carry your words. Tonight, in an inn, an old scholar is reading them aloud to a crowd, as proof the old king was blessed. People are nodding.

choices.text: Stand up and say it was a lie

effects.log: You stand up and say it, in front of everyone: you were paid, you saw nothing. The inn goes silent. The scholar is furious, then curious, then writes it down. That night, for the first time in years, you sleep without dreaming of the golden eye. In the morning the inn's floor is warm under your bare feet.

choices.text: Say nothing, and pay back the thirty taels to the temple

effects.log: You say nothing. In the morning you take thirty taels, every coin, to the temple poor-box. It does not undo anything. But walking out of the temple gate, you feel the ground under you level out, like a scale settling, and you understand that something has been keeping an account, and that it is kinder than you thought.

events.text: You have been made guardian to {npc}, the crown heir, a quiet youngster of fifteen who reads too much. The old king is dying. Tonight you find {npc} alone in the dark throne hall, lying flat on the floor in front of the throne, ear to the stones. "Something is talking under here," {npc} whispers. "It asked me a question."

choices.text: Ask what the question was

effects.log: "It asked: what will you set down?" {npc} says. "Not what will I carry. What will I set down." You lie down beside {npc} on the cold floor and listen. Nothing, at first. Then, very far below, a breath, slow as a season, and the stones under your cheek go warm. You stay there together until the lamps burn out.

choices.text: Say it is the wind under the floor

effects.log: "Wind under the floor," you say, and lift {npc} up. {npc} lets you, politely, and says nothing. But the next night you find {npc} there again, and the next, and on the third you lie down too, to prove it is the wind, and it is not the wind.

events.text: The old king is dead, and the succession is a knife-edge: an uncle with an army, a faction of ministers, and {npc}, the rightful heir, who has decided, against all advice, to give the regency to a council of elders and not to sit on the throne until twenty. "The voice says the throne is heavier than I know," {npc} says. "I believe it."

choices.text: Back {npc}: guard the council with your life

ok.log: The uncle's guard come for the council by night. You hold the doors of the elders' hall till dawn. The uncle, seeing the city stay quiet, goes back to the provinces. The council rules, badly at first, then well. And on the day {npc} turns twenty and sits on the throne at last, the whole hall feels the floor settle, like a load shared.

fail.log: The uncle's guard break the doors and you go down under three of them. But when they reach the inner hall, the floor of the elders' hall will not let them cross: it heaves, buckles and throws them back, and they run. {npc} nurses you through the winter personally. (-12 health)

choices.text: Argue with {npc}: a weak throne invites the uncle

effects.log: You argue all night. {npc} listens to every word, then says: "You are right that it is dangerous. The voice is right that it is heavy. I will take your guard and its advice." {npc} sets up the council and sits on the throne both, sharing every decision. It is slow and clumsy and nobody starves.

events.text: {npc} has reigned twenty years, and well. Tonight {npc} sends for you, alone, to the throne hall, and lies down on the floor before the throne like the child you first found there, and pats the stones. "It has stopped talking," {npc} says. "I think it means I do not need it any more. Is that good or bad?"

choices.text: Say: it is the best thing a ruler could hear

effects.log: "The best," you say. "It means you set enough down." {npc} laughs, the way {npc} used to as a youngster, and lies there a long while with one hand flat on the warm stone, saying goodbye. The kingdom goes on. Nobody remembers afterwards which year the throne room stopped feeling heavy.

choices.text: Lie down too, and listen together

effects.log: You lie down beside {npc} on the floor. Silence. Then, very faint, a single slow breath, far below, like someone falling asleep content. {npc} squeezes your hand. Neither of you says anything. The lamps burn down. It is one of the best nights of your life.

events.text: The old royal tutor has three royal pupils and a king too ill to choose an heir. The tutor has heard that you, of all people, once felt the ground answer you. Tonight the tutor takes you to the palace courtyard with three name tablets. "Ask it," the tutor says. "Let it choose. Then nobody can quarrel."

choices.text: Lay the three tablets on the ground and wait

effects.log: You lay them down. All night, nothing. At dawn all three tablets are warm, exactly as warm as each other. The tutor stares at them, then sits down on the steps and laughs till coughing. "Of course," the tutor says. "Of course it will not choose for us. Choosing is the job."

choices.text: Refuse: a ruler chosen by a dragon is not chosen

effects.log: "If it chooses, they will rule as its puppet," you say. "Choose them yourself, and teach them to listen." The tutor is angry, then ashamed, then grateful, all within an hour. The tutor sets the three a single question each and judges the answers. The one who asks a question back is chosen.

events.text: The chosen heir has come to you, the old tutor's friend, in secret. "They say a yellow dragon will come to the palace if my reign is blessed," the heir says. "And leave if it is not. How do I make it come?"

choices.text: Say: do not try to make it come; make it unnecessary

effects.log: "Do not try to make it come," you say. "Rule so well it is not needed." The heir looks bewildered, then, slowly, very thoughtful. Years later a minister tells you the heir had the sentence carved on a beam of the council hall, where everyone could see it, and nobody could reach it to take it down.

choices.text: Say: be fair at the market scales first; it starts there

effects.log: "Start with the market scales," you say. "Every one in the kingdom. Then the tax measures. Then the granary ladles." The heir writes it down. The first act of the new reign is a commission on weights and measures, which the court finds hilariously dull, and the farmers, for the first time in a century, do not.

events.text: {npc}, an alchemist of the court, has been ordered by the king to carve a royal seal of jade with a dragon's power in it, "so every decree carries the weight of the centre." {npc} has found a way: at noon on the solstice, a long golden shadow falls across the palace courtyard that belongs to no building. Cut the jade along the shadow, and the shadow is in the jade. {npc} needs a guard while it is measured.

choices.text: Guard {npc}, and watch closely

effects.log: You guard {npc} at noon. The shadow comes: long, coiled, golden, lying across the stones like something asleep in the sun. {npc} measures it with a knotted cord. As the cord touches it, the whole courtyard goes cold, and every bird on the roofs falls silent, and you know with absolute certainty that you are helping to do something wrong.

choices.text: Step on the shadow before {npc} can measure it

effects.log: You walk out into the courtyard and stand on the shadow, in the middle, as if by accident. It is warm under your feet, and it moves, very slightly, out from under you, and fades. {npc} curses you for a fool. You apologise very sincerely. Next solstice, you think, you will be here again.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whose decrees the seal will carry

effects.log: "The king's," {npc} says. "And the next king's. And the next." "Every king's?" you ask. "Even a cruel one?" {npc} is quiet a long time. "A seal does not choose," {npc} says at last. "That is the point of a seal." {npc} measures anyway. But {npc}'s hands shake on the cord.

events.text: The jade is cut. {npc} the alchemist has carved the seal in the shape of a coiled dragon, and tonight the binding is to be done: the measured shadow called down into the stone. You are guarding the workshop door. Inside, {npc} is chanting, and the ground under the whole palace has begun, very slowly, to shake.

choices.text: Break in and stop the binding

ok.log: You break in. {npc} fights like a cornered cat, cord and knife, and you take both. The jade seal cracks across, right through the dragon's neck, with a sound like a bell. The palace stops shaking. {npc} sits down among the shards and says, very quietly: "Thank you. I could not stop myself."

fail.log: You break in and {npc} throws something that burns and you go down. But the binding fails anyway: the seal on the bench cracks across the neck by itself, with a sound like a bell, as if something had simply refused. {npc} kneels among the shards, weeping, and binds your burns. (-10 health)

choices.text: Stay at the door, as ordered

effects.log: You stay at the door.
