The shaking stops at midnight. {npc} comes out grey and old, carrying a seal of green jade that is far too heavy for its size and warm, horribly warm, like a living thing. "It is done," {npc} says. Neither of you can look at it. The next decree it stamps is a new tax.

events.text: The jade seal has stamped twenty years of decrees, each a little harder than the last. Now a new young king has asked, privately, whether you know of any way to free what is in it. The seal sits on a cushion between you, warm as a sleeping cat, and very sad.

choices.text: Carry it back to the courtyard at noon on the solstice

effects.log: At noon on the solstice you set the seal on the stones of the palace courtyard, in the sun. Nothing; then a shadow seeps out of the jade, long and golden, and lies along the stones, and stretches, the way a stiff creature stretches after twenty years in a box, and sinks into the ground. The jade is only jade now. The young king keeps it on a desk as a paperweight, and uses an ordinary seal.

choices.text: Advise the king to break it before the whole court

effects.log: The young king breaks the seal before the assembled court with a mallet, in one blow. It cracks with a sound like a bell, and every lamp in the hall flares gold for a breath. Every decree it stamped is reviewed that year. Some are kept. Most are not. The court learns that a seal can be broken, which is not the lesson anyone expected.

events.text: In the great temple of the capital stands a statue cast from gold and iron that, they say, came on a ship with no crew from a western king who could not cast it himself. The statue weeps before disasters. Today, while you are praying, it weeps, and the tears run down to the floor and puddle, and the puddle is warm.

choices.text: Warn the city: something is coming

effects.log: You run to the magistrate of the capital, who laughs, and then, when you insist, sends criers round the wards just in case. Three days later the river breaks its banks in the night. Because of the criers, the lower wards are already on the roofs. You are not thanked, exactly. But the magistrate sends a boat for you personally.

choices.text: Kneel and touch the warm tears

effects.log: You touch them. They are not the statue's tears. You know it at once, the way you know whose hand is on your shoulder in the dark: they are coming up from under the floor, through the statue, from something under the temple that is sad about what is coming and cannot stop it. You leave the temple shaking. Three days later the river floods.

events.text: The statue is weeping again, harder than anyone has ever seen. The monks are frightened. An old monk takes you aside and says that the statue only weeps because the thing under the temple weeps, and the thing under the temple only weeps when the king does something unforgivable. "Go to the palace," the monk says. "Find out what."

choices.text: Go to the palace and find out

ok.log: It takes you a week of bribes and back stairs. The king has signed an order to empty three villages for a royal hunting park. You get the order to the queen dowager, who gets it to the king's face, in council. The order is torn up. The statue's face is dry by the next morning, and the monks say it is smiling, a little.

fail.log: You find nothing in time. The order to clear three villages for a hunting park goes out. The statue weeps for a month. Then the hunting park floods, every year, from springs that come up out of the dry ground, and the king gives up on it, and the villagers come back. The statue stops weeping.

choices.text: Sit with the statue and let it weep

effects.log: You sit with it all night, the warm tears running past your knees. It seems to help, somehow, to be sat with. In the morning a palace messenger comes to the temple, white-faced, with a royal apology for something the king will not name, and an offering of rice for the poor. The statue's face dries.

events.text: On the wall of the great temple, a painter of old painted a pine so true that birds flew at it to perch, and hit the wall, and fell stunned. The paint has faded; the birds stopped coming years ago. Now a young painter, {npc}, has been hired to repaint it, and has asked you, of all people, to stand and watch for birds.

choices.text: Stand and watch, all season

effects.log: You stand and watch all season while {npc} paints. Not one bird. {npc} is in despair. On the last day you notice what {npc} has not: the ground under the wall is cold. Under the rest of the temple it is warm, but here, cold, as if whatever lived under the old pine had moved away. You tell {npc}. {npc} stops painting and thinks.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to paint the ground under it too

effects.log: "Paint the ground," you say, without knowing why. "The roots. The earth they go into." {npc} looks at you strangely, and paints a band of warm yellow earth at the foot of the pine, with the roots going down into it. The next morning a sparrow flies at the wall, and hits it, and falls, and gets up, offended. {npc} cheers so loudly the monks come running.

events.text: {npc} the painter, older now, has written: "I cannot make the birds come back. I have repainted the pine six times. The old master never told anyone the secret. Come and look at it with me one more time."

choices.text: Go, and put your hand on the wall

effects.log: You put your palm on the painted trunk. Cold plaster. You leave it there a long time. Slowly the plaster warms under your hand, from below, from the ground, as if something had heard you knock. {npc} puts a hand beside yours. By evening the wall is warm to the top branch. The next morning the birds come back, and fall, and get up, and {npc} sits down in the courtyard and laughs and cries.

choices.text: Tell {npc}: the secret is that the world believed it

effects.log: "The old master did not paint a pine," you say. "The old master painted what the ground under the temple wanted a pine to be, and the ground agreed." {npc} stares at you. Then {npc} goes and sits on the ground under the wall for three days, doing nothing, and on the fourth day paints one branch, and a bird lands on it.

events.text: The throne hall is being rebuilt, and the court painters are painting a pair of golden dragons on the ceiling over the throne. They have come to blows over the claws: four claws, says one, as a vassal king must; five, says another, quietly, as kings always have; seven, says the youngest, because this king will bow to nobody. They have asked an outsider to settle it. You.

choices.text: Say: four, and keep the peace with the empire

effects.log: "Four," you say. The old painter beams; the young one sulks. The dragons go up with four claws each. That night, alone in the hall, you could swear one of the painted dragons is looking at you with mild, patient amusement, as if to say: you think I count my own claws?

choices.text: Say: seven, and let the king be a king

effects.log: "Seven," you say. The youngest whoops. The old painters go pale. The dragons go up with seven claws each, which is either treason or a declaration, and in the end, years later, it turns out to be a declaration. The youngest painter sends you a sketch of the claws every New Year.

choices.text: Say: ask the dragon

effects.log: "Ask the dragon," you say. They laugh. But the youngest leaves the claws unpainted overnight, as a joke, and in the morning there are faint golden marks on the ceiling where the claws would be: five on one dragon, seven on the other, as if pressed up from inside the wood. Nobody argues after that. They paint them in.

events.text: The throne hall with the golden dragons on the ceiling is finished. The king has invited the painters, and you, to see it before the court does. The throne is empty. The dragons on the ceiling are wonderful. Then the youngest painter grabs your arm and points: one of them has moved.

choices.text: Look up for a long time

effects.log: You look up. The painted dragon has turned its head, just a little, toward the empty throne, the way an old servant turns toward a door when a footstep comes. It does not move again. But for the rest of that reign, every new minister is brought here once, alone, to stand under it, and nobody will say why.

choices.text: Bow to the empty throne

effects.log: You bow, not to the dragons, to the empty chair. The painters, after a moment, bow too. When you straighten, the painted dragon has turned its head back to where it was, satisfied, and the hall feels warm. The king hears of it and is oddly moved, and for the rest of the reign bows to the throne each morning before sitting on it.

events.text: You have ridden with {npc} for thirty years: the founder of a new kingdom in the north, who crossed a river with nothing and built a capital out of a camp. Now {npc} is old, and dying, and has asked to be carried up the hill east of the capital at dawn. "The dragon will come," {npc} says. "It told me so when I was young."

choices.text: Carry {npc} up the hill yourself

effects.log: You carry {npc} up on your back, as you once carried {him} wounded out of a battle. At the top {npc} stands, by some last strength, and looks east. The clouds open, gold, and something vast and golden comes down through them, slowly, with its head bowed, and stops above the hill, and waits.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the dragon said, all those years ago

effects.log: "It said: build a house that can stand without me," {npc} says. "Then I will come for you." {npc} laughs, weakly. "I have tried for forty years. Let us see if I managed." You carry {npc} up the hill. At dawn the clouds over it turn gold, and part.

events.text: On the hill at dawn the golden dragon has come down and lowered its great head to the grass in front of {npc}. {npc} turns to you. "Come with me," {npc} says. "It will carry two. I asked."

choices.text: Stay: someone has to tell the capital

effects.log: "Someone has to tell them," you say. {npc} nods, and clasps your hands, and steps onto the dragon's head, and the two of them rise into the dawn together, slowly, not looking back, until they are only a gold mark in the east. You walk down the hill and tell the capital. Nobody believes you except the children, and the children are right.

choices.text: Help {npc} up, and stay

effects.log: You help {npc} onto the great golden head, as you once helped {him} onto horses. The dragon's eye, the size of a pond, looks at you once, kindly. Then it rises with the founder on its back into the dawn. You stand on the hill till the sun is high. The grass where the dragon lay stays green all winter.

choices.text: Ask the dragon one question first

effects.log: "Is the house strong enough?" you ask the dragon. It looks at you for a long moment, and then at the capital below, and then, very slightly, it nods. {npc} laughs out loud, and climbs on, and they go up together into the gold. You never forget that nod. You carry it down the hill like a jar of water you must not spill.

events.text: Years after the founder rose from the eastern hill, the founder's grandchild, now on the throne, asks you to come up the hill at dawn with the court, as a witness, for the anniversary. The court is restless. A war party wants a war, and is using the founder's name.

choices.text: Tell the court what the dragon said: build a house that can stand without me

effects.log: You tell them, on the hill, at dawn: the dragon did not come for a conqueror. It came for someone who built a house that could stand without a dragon. The war party is silent. The grandchild on the throne looks east a long time, and then dismisses the war council, and builds roads that year instead.

choices.text: Say nothing; let the sunrise speak

effects.log: You stand silent with the court. The sun comes up. And the clouds over the eastern hill turn gold, and for a moment, just a moment, everyone sees two shapes in them, a great coiled one and a small one riding on its head. The war party goes very quiet. There is no war that year, or the next.

events.text: You are riding with a young archer, a runaway prince with a price on {his} head and hunters a hill behind, and you have come to a river too wide and fast to ford. {npc} draws rein at the bank and calls out to the water, in a great voice, the name of {his} mother's people and {his} father's, and asks to cross.

choices.text: Turn and hold the hunters off

ok.log: You turn and hold the bank against the riders while behind you the river breaks, and the backs of turtles rise in a line across it, a bridge of shells. {npc} shouts to you; you break off and run, and the two of you cross on the turtles' backs, and the moment you are over, the bridge sinks. The hunters sit their horses on the far bank, staring.

fail.log: The riders cut through you on the bank. {npc} turns back for you, hauls you up behind, and spurs the horse onto the river itself, onto a road of turtles' backs rising out of the water. Behind you the bridge sinks. You lose a lot of blood and come to on the far shore with the river between you and the hunters. (-9 health)

choices.text: Call out with {npc}

effects.log: You call out with {npc}, your own name and your own people, feeling ridiculous. The river breaks. Turtles, hundreds, rise in a line across it, shell to shell, and you ride over them in the dusk with the hunters shouting behind. The far bank is warm under the horses' hooves, oddly warm. "Here," {npc} says. "I will build here."

events.text: {npc} has built a fortress on the far bank, and a camp around it, and a town around the camp, and now people call it a capital and {npc} a king. Tonight {npc} has asked you up to the wall to look at the hills. "The ground here is warm," {npc} says. "It has been warm since the night we crossed. I think something chose this place, not me."

choices.text: Say: then build something worth being chosen

effects.log: "Then build something worth it," you say. {npc} builds: a fair court, a granary, a law that a guest is sacred. Years later, the night {npc} founds the royal altar, a yellow light rises over the hill east of the city and hangs there till dawn, and the whole town sees it, and the chroniclers write it down.

choices.text: Say: chosen or not, you crossed

effects.log: "Chosen or not," you say, "you crossed. You called out to a river and it answered. That was you." {npc} laughs, and looks less tired. That winter the warm ground under the capital keeps the wells from freezing, and the young king walks the walls every night saying thank you to something nobody else can see.

events.text: The horsemen from the steppe have taken the capital, and tonight they are coming for the great temple and its wooden pagoda nine storeys high. The abbot has asked you, the strongest guest in the temple, to carry out the scriptures: the oldest copies in the kingdom, an armful of them. The first torches are already at the gate.

choices.text: Carry the scriptures out through the back

effects.log: You carry them out through the back gate and up the hill, the abbot stumbling behind you. Behind you the pagoda catches, storey by storey, and goes up like a torch the height of a mountain, and the whole sky is red. And under it, through the smoke, from the foundation stones, a gold light comes up, and stays, and does not burn.

choices.text: Hold the gate while the monks carry them

ok.log: You hold the gate. It is the longest fight of your life, and by the end the horsemen have stopped trying to come through you and are riding round, and every monk and every scroll is out on the hill. Then the pagoda goes up, nine storeys of fire. Under the fire, at the foundations, a gold light, unburned.

fail.log: You hold the gate till they bring you down. The monks get out with the scrolls while you lie in the gate tower with the smoke rolling over you. Somebody drags you out. From the hill you watch the pagoda burn, and under it, through the smoke, a gold light that does not go out. (-12 health)

events.text: Months after the burning, you go back to the ruin with the old abbot. Nothing is left of the pagoda: sixty-four foundation stones in the ash, and the great centre stone, its socket full of rainwater. The abbot sits on the centre stone and will not get up. "It stayed," the abbot says. "Feel. It stayed."

choices.text: Put your hand on the centre stone

effects.log: You put your hand on it. Warm. Under the warm, a slow rise and fall, like breathing. The thing that held up the pagoda for six hundred years did not leave when the pagoda burned. It is still down there, holding up nothing, keeping its place. The abbot weeps. You sit with the abbot until dark.

choices.text: Promise the abbot the scriptures will be copied

effects.log: "They will be copied," you say, "every one, a hundred times." The abbot nods. You spend the next ten years seeing it done, in temples all over the kingdom. Every copy, by the abbot's wish, is first laid for one night on the centre stone, in the rain. Every copy comes back warm.

events.text: The horsemen have taken the great temple's bell, a bronze monster the weight of fifty oxen, and are dragging it on rollers over the low pass to the sea, to ship it home. You have been taken as a labourer. The general in charge, {npc}, rides beside the bell every day and looks at it, and you have heard {npc} argue with the other commanders that it should not be melted.

choices.text: Talk to {npc} at the evening fire

effects.log: "It rings when nobody strikes it," {npc} tells you at the fire. "At night. Low. The men are afraid of it. The others want it melted for arrowheads. I want to take it home and hang it." {npc} looks at the bell. "I do not want to be the one who melted the voice of a country."

choices.text: Slow the rollers, a little, every day

effects.log: You slow them, a little, every day: a roller set crooked, a rope frayed. {npc} sees, and says nothing, and once, when an officer whips you for it, {npc} stops the whip. The bell goes slower and slower. On the pass the earth itself seems to hold it back, warm and heavy, like a hand on a sleeve.

events.text: The bell has reached the river mouth on the East Sea. A ship is waiting. {npc} the general has been overruled: the bell will be shipped home and melted. As they swing it out on the loading ropes over the grey water, the ropes begin to creak, and the ground under the shore starts to shake.

choices.text: Cut the ropes

ok.log: You fight your way to the windlass and cut. The bell drops into the sea with a sound you will hear for the rest of your life. {npc} rides down to the water's edge and sits a long time on the horse, then turns to you and says only: "Good." And lets you go. That night, in a storm, the bell rings under the waves.

fail.log: The guards beat you down before you reach the windlass. But the ground shakes once more, hard, and the ropes part by themselves, and the bell goes into the sea. {npc} looks at the water, and at you, and quietly orders you released. That night, in the storm, the bell rings under the waves. (-9 health)

choices.text: Stand by {npc} and watch

effects.log: You stand beside {npc}. The shaking grows. The ropes snap one by one, as if something below were pulling, and the bell drops into the grey sea and is gone. {npc} lets out a long breath. "Something did not want it to go," {npc} says. On stormy nights for the rest of your life, near the coast, you hear it ringing under the waves.

events.text: The kingdom is falling apart: three claimants, a famine, a war on the border. The ministers of the court, at their wits' end, have come to you, a master strong enough to be heard in heaven, with a crown on a cushion. "Take this to the Yellow Dragon," they beg. "Ask it to rule us. Nobody will quarrel with a dragon."

choices.text: Carry the crown to the dragon

effects.log: You carry it up through the clouds to where the great golden shape lies coiled over the kingdom, so vast its back is a range of hills. You hold out the crown. The dragon looks at it a long time. Then one eye, the size of a lake, closes and opens: a slow blink. It does not take the crown. Below, very faintly, you feel the whole kingdom lean a little less.

choices.text: Refuse to carry it

effects.log: "A dragon on the throne," you tell the ministers, "and you will never learn to rule yourselves." They are furious. They go away. A month later three of them come back, one from each claimant's party, without a crown, and ask you to sit with them while they talk. You do. It takes a year.

events.text: The ministers have sent for you again. The famine is over; the border is quiet; two of the three claimants have made peace with the third. And every night since, a great warm weight has settled over the palace, not crushing, just there, like a hand on a shoulder. The ministers want to know what it means.

choices.text: Say: it is holding you up, not ruling you

effects.log: "It is holding you up," you say, "while you learn to stand. One day you will not feel it, and that will be the day you are ready." The ministers write it down. Thirty years later, an old minister writes to you: "I did not feel it this spring. Nobody did. We are fine."

choices.text: Go up and thank it, for them

effects.log: You go up through the clouds and thank it, for all of them. The great golden shape stirs, and settles, and a warm wind goes down over the whole kingdom, and in every field the barley bows the same way at once. When you come down, the ministers are standing on the terrace in the wind with their hats off, bowing to nothing in particular.

events.text: {npc}, a grandmaster of the age, has announced to the whole murim that {npc} will challenge the Dragon of the Between-Seasons to a duel on the highest peak, in the eighteen days before autumn, for the right to choose one season's weather for {his} province. {npc} has asked you to stand as witness.

choices.text: Stand witness, and say nothing

effects.log: You stand witness on the peak. {npc} challenges the sky. The sky, after a long time, answers: a golden shape uncoils over the summit, vast and calm, and simply waits. {npc} strikes. The blow goes into the dragon like a stone into a field, and the field is not hurt. {npc} strikes all day. At sunset {npc} sits down, exhausted, and the dragon lowers its head, politely, as if to ask: are you done?

choices.text: Try to talk {npc} out of it

ok.log: You talk for three days. "One season's weather for your province," you say, "is another province's drought." {npc} goes very quiet, and then laughs, and withdraws the challenge publicly. The murim is scandalised. That autumn the weather is fair everywhere, and {npc} sends you a jar of plum wine with a note: "Fair everywhere. Fine."

fail.log: {npc} will not hear it. The duel goes ahead. {npc} strikes at the golden shape over the peak all day and every blow sinks in like rain into dry earth. At sunset {npc} sits down in the dust, and the dragon lowers its head, kindly, and goes. {npc} does not speak for a week.

choices.text: Challenge {npc} first, to spare the dragon the trouble

ok.log: You meet {npc} on the peak first. It is a great fight, the kind the murim talks about for a generation, and at the end of it you stand and {npc} sits. "Why?" {npc} asks. "Because it would not have fought back," you say. "And you would have learned nothing." Over the peak, the sky is very slightly gold, as if amused.

fail.log: {npc} beats you, fairly, on the peak, and then turns to challenge the sky anyway, and the sky sends down a golden calm so complete that {npc}'s blows simply stop in the air. {npc} carries you down the mountain. Neither of you mentions the weather again. (-12 health)

events.text: {npc} the grandmaster has been brooding on the peak since the duel. Now {npc} writes: "I asked it for one season. It gave me none, and every province had a fair year. I want to ask it why. Come with me."

choices.text: Go, and let {npc} ask

effects.log: You climb with {npc}. On the peak {npc} asks the empty sky, simply: "Why?" A warm wind comes up from every side at once, from the four directions, and meets in the middle, where you are both standing, and stops. {npc} stands in the stillness a long time. "Oh," {npc} says at last. "It is the middle. It cannot choose one side. It would fall."

choices.text: Tell {npc}: you already know why

effects.log: "You know why," you write back. "It holds all the seasons at once. One season for you is a hole in the wheel." {npc} does not reply for a year. Then a parcel comes: a sword, {npc}'s own, and a note: "I have taken up farming. Everything is very slow and very even. I like it."

events.text: A summons has come to you from beyond the clouds, in a grey clerk's careful hand: the four guardians of the directions request a human witness, of the highest realm below heaven, "to see the centre filled, and say so to the world below." You go up. On the terrace of cloud the four banners stand at the four sides, and the middle is empty, and warm.

choices.text: Stand at the edge and watch

effects.log: You stand at the edge. For a long time nothing. Then the light begins to gather in the middle, the way dawn gathers in a valley: gold, from nowhere, slowly, until there is something there, coiled, vast, quiet, and the four banners at the four sides stand still for the first time in a thousand years. You do not breathe. Nobody does. When it is done, the clerk touches your sleeve and says: "Now go and tell them."

choices.text: Kneel at the edge, as the four do

effects.log: You kneel. You are not sure the four guardians kneel, exactly, but their banners bow, one by one, east, west, south, north. In the middle the light gathers into a great golden shape that settles, and turns its head, and looks along the circle at each of them, and then, last, at you, a human at the edge. You will never be able to say what was in that look. Only that it was not surprise.

events.text: You have come down from the cloud terrace to tell the world below what you saw. Nobody wants to hear it. The sects want to know which of them the centre favours; the kings want to know if it means a new dynasty; the shamans want to know which colour flag to raise.

choices.text: Tell everyone the same thing: it favours nobody

effects.log: "It favours nobody," you say, to the sects, to the kings, to the shamans. "It holds everybody up. That is what the centre is." Most of them go away disappointed. A few go away thinking. One old shaman raises a yellow flag at the next rite, alone in the middle of the yard, and sits under it, and does not dance at all.

choices.text: Say nothing, and go home to your own village

effects.log: You say nothing to any of them. You go home to the village where you were born and help with the harvest. On the threshing yard, at noon, the packed earth is warm under your feet, warmer than the sun could make it, and you laugh out loud, alone, with a flail in your hands.

events.text: You have reached the height of the world below, and you can feel what holds it up: under everything, under every harvest and every war and every king, something carrying the weight, patient and enormous and very tired. Tonight, on a bare hilltop, you sit down and lay your palms on the earth and offer to carry some of it.

choices.text: Take a share, and hold it

ok.log: It comes up into your hands: not a weight exactly, more a responsibility, a hundred villages' harvests, a dozen quarrels, a sickly heir. It is unbearable for an hour and then, slowly, bearable. Under the earth, something lets out a breath it has been holding for a century. You hold your share all night. At dawn you stand up lighter than you have ever been, because you were trusted.

fail.log: It comes up into your hands, and it is too much. You hold it as long as you can, which is not long, and then it goes back down, gently, as if taken back by a hand that expected this. You lie on the hilltop gasping. The earth under you is warm, and patient, and you could swear, not disappointed. (-10 health)

choices.text: Ask what it would have you carry

effects.log: You ask. For a long time, nothing. Then, very faint, an answer in the warmth under your palms: one village. Not a kingdom. One village, by the river, where the elders quarrel and the granary leaks. Carry that. You laugh, because it is so small, and then you go to the village, and it takes you ten years, and it is the hardest thing you have ever done.

events.text: Years after you took a share of the weight, you notice that you have not felt it for a while. Your village is well; the elders sit together; the granary is sound. And a young martial artist from the village has come to you, frowning, saying: "I feel something under the ground. Heavy. As if it wanted help."

choices.text: Teach the youngster to carry a little of it

effects.log: You take the youngster up the bare hill and show them how: palms on the earth, ask, listen, take only what is offered. The youngster carries one household's worth, and staggers, and laughs. That is how it is passed, you realise: not all at once, from the centre to one great hero, but a household at a time, to anyone who will put their hands down and ask.

choices.text: Say: then it trusts you; go and ask what it wants

effects.log: "Then it trusts you," you say. "Go and ask it." The youngster goes. A month later the youngster comes back, glowing, having mended a ferry, settled a quarrel and buried a stranger. "It was so small," the youngster says. "Every time I asked, it was something so small." You nod. It always is.

events.text: The small kingdom has been humiliated for a generation by its great neighbours. Now its king has decided to stop being anyone's vassal: to sacrifice to heaven and earth at a round altar, sit on a golden chair, and wear yellow, the colour of the centre. You are hired to stand behind the chair. The ministers are practising their shout: not a thousand years, but ten thousand.

choices.text: Stand behind the chair and keep your eyes open

effects.log: You stand behind the golden chair through the whole rite. The ministers shout ten thousand years, and it rolls off the altar like thunder. Under your feet the stones of the round altar go warm, and stay warm, as if something had come to stand behind the chair with you, and approved, though not entirely of the king.

choices.text: Tell the king, privately, that yellow is heavy

effects.log: "Yellow is heavy," you say to the king in the robing tent. "It is not a colour you wear. It is a weight you carry." The king looks at you a long time, tired, proud and very frightened. "I know," the king says. "That is why I am wearing it. Somebody has to." You stand behind the chair. The altar is warm.

events.text: The empire of the golden chair did not last; the great neighbours came anyway, as everyone knew they would. Years later you walk into the old throne hall. The chair is empty. On the ceiling above it, the pair of golden dragons look down at nothing.

choices.text: Sit on the floor before the empty chair a while

effects.log: You sit on the floor before the empty chair. It is very quiet. After a long time you feel it: a faint warmth from above, from the painted ceiling, like a lamp left burning in an empty house so whoever comes home will find it lit. You bow to the chair. You leave the door open behind you.

choices.text: Say to the ceiling: the king tried

effects.log: "The king tried," you say to the painted dragons. "Ten thousand years. It lasted thirteen. But the king tried." Dust drifts down through the light. One of the painted dragons seems, for a moment, to lower its head, the way a person nods at a grave. You go out into the sun.

events.text: An envoy of the Jade court has come to the guardians' terrace to audit the centre: its accounts, its harvests, its kings carried up, its weight. You have been assigned to the envoy as an escort and, it turns out, as someone to complain to. "There is nothing here," the envoy says, rattling an abacus. "No ledger. No clerk. No record. How do I audit nothing?"

choices.text: Help the envoy look

effects.log: You help. You look for a month, under every cloud. There is no ledger. But every harvest below came in, every hand-over of the seasons happened on time, every king carried up arrived. The envoy, at the end, writes one line in the Jade court's book: "Audited the centre. Found nothing to audit." Then, after a pause: "Commend."

choices.text: Tell the envoy: the record is the world below

effects.log: "The record is the world below," you say, and take the envoy to the edge of the terrace and show it: the fields, the roads, the square with its honest scale, the villages with jars behind the houses. The envoy looks for a long time. "That is not a ledger," the envoy says. "No," you say. "It is better." The envoy goes home without writing anything at all.

events.text: The Jade court's envoy has come back, embarrassed. The court did not accept "nothing to audit". Now the envoy must find one fault in the centre, any fault, or be demoted. "Help me," the envoy says. "Just one."

choices.text: Find one honest fault together

effects.log: You search together, honestly, for a season. In the end you find one: in a single village below, a single teoju jar has been forgotten for three tenth months running, and the house above it has been unlucky. The envoy writes it down, and then, unexpectedly, goes down to the village in disguise and changes the rice. The court accepts the fault. The house's luck returns.

choices.text: Refuse to invent one

effects.log: "I will not invent one," you say. The envoy is demoted, to a minor post in the Upper Realm's granaries. A century later you visit. The envoy is happier than you have ever seen anyone, among the grain, and every measure in the granary is honest, and the floor is warm.

events.text: The council of the four directions has called you to testify. A king below was carried up to heaven on the Yellow Dragon's back from the hill east of the capital, and now the White Tiger's banner says the king was cruel in youth and should not have been carried. You lived below in that king's day, and you are called as one who remembers it.

choices.text: Testify to the cruelty, and to the change

effects.log: You tell it all: the cruel prince, the burned village, and then the long middle of the reign, the granaries, the roads, the pardons, the old king weeping at the grave of the village. The council is silent. Then the golden glow at the centre stirs, and a few words come from it, dry and quiet: "I carried the end of the life. Not the beginning." The White Tiger's banner dips.

choices.text: Say: judge the king by the kingdom left behind

effects.log: "Look at the kingdom the king left," you say. "Look at it now." The council looks down through the clouds: fields, roads, a fair court, a grandchild on the throne who listens. The White Tiger's banner hangs still for a long time. Then the clerk writes: "Carried rightly." From the centre comes a faint warmth, like thanks.

events.text: After your testimony, the carried king has come to find you in heaven: very old, very quiet, an immortal of no great rank who tends a small garden on a cloud. "You told them about the village," the old king says. "Nobody else ever did. Thank you."

choices.text: Sit with the old king in the garden

effects.log: You sit in the small garden together. The old king grows only rice, a few rows, in yellow earth carried up from the hill east of the old capital. "It reminds me," the old king says, "where I was picked up from." You eat a bowl of that rice together. It is the best rice in heaven, and nobody else knows.

choices.text: Ask what the ride up was like

effects.log: "Warm," the old king says. "And slow. The dragon went slowly so I could look back. I looked back the whole way, at the capital, getting smaller. Then it said one thing, the only thing it ever said to me: you may stop carrying it now." The old king is quiet a long time. "I wept all the way to heaven."

events.text: {npc}, a heavenly immortal of quiet reputation, stands every dawn at the eastern edge of the terraces, looking down at a particular hill. Today {npc} has asked you to stand there too. "I was a king once," {npc} says. "I was carried up from that hill. Every dawn I check it is still there."
events.arc: The King from the Eastern Hill

choices.text: Stand with {npc} every dawn for a season

effects.log: You stand with {npc} every dawn for a season. The hill is always there. On the last morning, a little gold light rises on it, very faint, as if something below were checking on {npc} too. {npc} laughs, delighted. "It does that," {npc} says. "Once a century. I think it is making sure I did not fall off."

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether the kingdom remembers

effects.log: "The kingdom forgot me in two hundred years," {npc} says, cheerful. "Quite right. But the hill remembers. Every dawn, someone in the town below climbs it, and does not know why." {npc} points: far down, a tiny figure climbing a green hill in the first light. "That one is my great-great-great-great-grandchild. No idea. Lovely."

events.text: {npc} has come to you troubled. Down below, on the eastern hill, the descendants of {npc}'s house are about to go to war with one another over the throne. "I may not interfere," {npc} says. "I am an immortal now. But you are younger here. Rules are looser for the young."
events.arc: The King from the Eastern Hill

choices.text: Go down and speak to both sides on the hill

ok.log: You go down to the eastern hill and call both princes up it at dawn, and their champions try you, and fail. Then you tell them the story of the founder carried up from this hill, and what the dragon said: build a house that can stand without me. The princes are quiet. They divide the work, not the kingdom. {npc}, watching from the clouds, weeps.

fail.log: The princes' champions try you on the hill and you lose, which up here is humiliating. But you tell the story anyway, bleeding, and the princes hear it, and so does the hill: it goes gold at dawn, and the princes kneel, and the war ends before it starts. {npc} brings you medicine personally. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell {npc}: trust the house you built

effects.log: "You built a house that could stand without you," you say. "Trust it." {npc} trusts it. It is the hardest month of {npc}'s immortal life. The princes argue, and nearly fight, and at the last moment their grandmother, a formidable old woman, bangs their heads together. {npc} laughs until {npc} has to sit down.

events.text: The clerks of heaven's almanac are in a panic: somebody has lost eighteen days. Between the end of summer and the start of autumn there is a gap in the great calendar, and nobody can find what goes in it, and below, the seasons are refusing to hand over. You have been seconded to help find them.

choices.text: Go down and look in a farmhouse yard

effects.log: You go down to the world below, to the first farmhouse you see, and stand in the yard in late summer. There they are: in the yellow earth, warm, unhurried, eighteen days lying in the soil like seed. You bring a handful of the earth up to heaven and lay it in the gap in the calendar. The scroll warms. Below, summer hands over to autumn, gently, the way a bowl is passed.

choices.text: Ask the clerks who usually keeps those days

effects.log: Nobody knows. You ask everyone. At last a very old clerk says: "The centre keeps them. Earth. It has no season of its own, so it holds the hand-overs." "And where is the centre?" you ask. The clerk shrugs: "Asleep, mostly." You go to the empty middle of the guardians' terrace and say, politely: "Excuse me. You dropped something." The calendar fills by morning.

events.text: The clerks of the almanac have made you an honorary keeper of the between-days, which as far as you can tell means you must go below at the end of each season and check on the earth. This season, in one valley, a lord is digging a great moat in the forbidden days.

choices.text: Go down and ask the lord to wait

effects.log: You go down as a travelling scholar and ask the lord, politely, to wait eighteen days. The lord laughs. You stay. You help dig, on the nineteenth day, and the moat goes in sweet and dry, and the lord, puzzled, has a shrine to the earth built at the corner of it. You write it up for the clerks. They are thrilled. They have never had a report before.

choices.text: Let it be; the earth will make its own point

effects.log: You let it be. The moat floods at once with yellow water that will not drain, and the lord's labourers sit on the bank for eighteen days, eating, because there is nothing else to do. On the nineteenth the water sinks away like a bath emptying. The lord learns. You write it up. The clerks find it very funny.

events.text: The Yellow Emperor of the Centre, the great golden one at the middle of everything, has asked to see you: an Immortal Sovereign, one of very few. Through a gap in heaven it shows you a young world, far off, scattered, its islands drifting, its seasons fighting, with nothing in the middle at all. "It needs a centre," the golden one says. Few words. "Would you be it?"

choices.text: Accept: go and be the middle of a world

effects.log: You accept. You go. It takes a thousand years. You do it the way you were shown, below, all your life: a house site, a jar, a yard, a crossroads, a square, a county, one thing at a time. The islands stop drifting. The seasons hand over. One day you notice that the young world does not need you to hold it, only to be there, and you understand, finally, what the golden one has been doing all along.

choices.text: Decline: a centre should grow from the world itself

effects.log: "A centre should grow out of its own world," you say, "or it will crush it." The golden one is silent a long time. Then it does something you have never seen: it laughs, very quietly, the sound of a field of barley in wind. "Good," it says. "That is the answer." Together you go and plant something in the middle of the young world: a lump of warm clay, the size of a fist.

choices.text: Ask: who taught you?

effects.log: "Who taught you?" you ask. The golden one considers this. "A farmhouse," it says at last. "A jar of rice. A family that changed the rice every tenth month and said a few words to the ground." It looks at you. "Mostly the few words." You go to the young world together, and find a farmhouse, and start there.

events.text: The young world is growing. In its middle, at the place you and the golden one both know, there is now a small farmhouse, a family, a jar behind the house with a straw cap. A child of that family has just stamped on the yard at the first full moon, and the yard has stamped back.

choices.text: Go down, as a traveller, and visit the family

effects.log: You go down as an old traveller and are given rice and a mat for the night. The child tells you, very seriously, that the yard stamps back. You say you believe it. In the morning you leave a single coin on the gatepost and bow to the house, not to the family, and go, and the child watches you all the way down the road.

choices.text: Watch from heaven, and leave it alone

effects.log: You watch from heaven and leave it alone. That is the hardest thing and the right one. The child grows. The house prospers. The clay under it warms, year by year, and one late summer, in the eighteen days before autumn, it beats, once, like a held breath let go. You sit very still in heaven and smile.

events.text: {npc}, an Immortal Sovereign of enormous power and very little patience, has set a throne in the exact middle of the guardians' terrace and announced that {npc} is now the centre. The four banners have been pushed to the edges. {npc} has summoned you, of all the sovereigns, to ask a question: "How does one become the centre of everything?"

choices.text: Answer honestly: you hold everything up, and are never thanked

effects.log: "You hold everything up," you say, "every harvest and every war, and you are never thanked, and in the end you set it all down, and nobody notices you have gone." {npc} stares at you. "That is not what I meant," {npc} says. "I know," you say. {npc} sits on the throne in the middle for a season, and the throne gets heavier, and heavier.

choices.text: Answer: you start with one jar of rice

effects.log: "You start with a jar of rice behind a farmhouse," you say, "and you keep one family lucky for a hundred years." {npc} laughs, a big cold laugh. "I am a Sovereign." "Yes," you say. "That is why it would be hard for you." {npc} stops laughing.

choices.text: Challenge {npc} to step off the centre

ok.log: You fight {npc} in the middle of the terrace, and it is an enormous fight, and the clouds split. You win by never moving from one spot, the way the ground wins. {npc}, beaten, steps off the centre, furious. The four banners slide back into place. Under the middle, very faint, something gold breathes out.

fail.log: {npc} beats you, thoroughly, in the middle of the terrace. But as {npc} turns to sit back down, the throne is not there. It has sunk into the cloud, quietly, like a stone into a pond, and the banners have slid back to their places, and the middle is empty and warm. {npc} stares at it a long time. (-14 health)

events.text: {npc}, the Sovereign who tried to sit in the centre, has come to your door, alone, without the dazzling robes. "The throne was so heavy," {npc} says. "I could not stand up. I could not think of anything but the weight. How does it bear it? The golden one. How?"

choices.text: Say: it shares it; take a share

effects.log: "It shares it," you say. "With anyone who asks. Go and ask." {npc} goes to the empty middle of the terrace and kneels, very awkwardly, and asks. For a long time, nothing. Then, from the warm cloud, something small: a single village below, a ferry that keeps sinking. {npc} goes down and mends the ferry, with {npc}'s own sovereign hands, and comes back changed.

choices.text: Say: it lets go, a little every year

effects.log: "It lets go," you say. "A little every year. That is the whole secret." {npc} thinks about it for a century. Then one day you hear {npc} has handed every one of {npc}'s fiefs to their own councils, and gone to grow rice on a small cloud, and has never been happier, and is still very impatient.

events.text: You are old, and it is time to hand the keeping of the jar behind the house to the next of the family. The straw cap has been rewoven more times than you can count. The rice inside has been changed every tenth month of your life. The youngest of the house is waiting, holding a basket of new rice, a little afraid of the jar.

choices.text: Kneel with the youngest and change the rice together

effects.log: You kneel together behind the house. You lift the cap; the old rice is warm, as always, and there is more of it than went in, as always. The youngest's eyes go round. You pour in the new rice together, and straighten the cap, and say the few words. The ground under your knees warms, and the youngest gasps, and laughs, and you know the jar is in good hands.

choices.text: Let the youngest do it alone while you watch from the step

effects.log: You sit on the kitchen step and watch. The youngest kneels, lifts the cap, hesitates, and then, without being told, says something to the jar, too quietly for you to hear. Whatever it was, the jar must have liked it: that winter the house has the best luck in the valley, and you never ask what was said.

events.text: The old scale in the square has read true for years. Now the beam has split, from age, and the market elders have come to you, since you are the one it is linked to, to ask what should be done.

choices.text: Have a new scale made, and hang the old one beside it

effects.log: A carpenter makes a new scale, plain and well balanced, and you hang it in the square beside the split old one. For a month the new scale reads like any scale: a little off, depending who leans. Then one morning it reads true, and stays true. The packed earth of the square is warm. The elders bow to both scales at New Year.

choices.text: Say: the market does not need it any more

effects.log: "Years of honest weights," you say. "The market has learned. Take it down." The elders are horrified. But they take it down, and the merchants go on weighing honestly, out of habit and pride and the memory of the grandmothers' silence. The ground of the square stays warm all the same.

events.text: You have kept the sixty-four stones for many late summers since the caretaker died. This year a royal survey has come to the ruin to measure it for the annals, and the surveyors want to lift the centre stone to see what is beneath.

choices.text: Ask them to measure around it, not under it

effects.log: You walk the surveyors round the site and tell them the whole story, the marsh, the palace, the pagoda, the burning. They measure the sixty-four stones, and the socket, and the rainwater in it, and leave the centre stone where it is. The annals record: "Centre stone: not lifted, at the request of its keeper." You are absurdly proud of that line.

choices.text: Let them lift it, and stand by

effects.log: They lever it up. Underneath there is only earth, packed and yellow, and warm as bread, and an empty hollow where a box once was. The surveyors put their hands on it in turn, without being asked, and go quiet. They lower the stone back gently. Nobody writes down the warmth. Everyone remembers it.

events.text: Every village in the county keeps a famine store now, with the key held by an elder, since the winter you guarded the granary. A young magistrate newly arrived wants to abolish them: untidy, unofficial, bad for the tax rolls.

choices.text: Take the young magistrate to the old granary at night

effects.log: You take the young magistrate to the old county granary at midnight and ask them to kneel and put a palm on the floor. Warm. Heavy, somehow, with all the winters it has held. You tell the story. The magistrate stays kneeling a long time, then gets up and goes home, and the famine stores stay.

choices.text: Gather the elders to speak for the stores

effects.log: You bring every elder of every village to the yamen with their keys on strings round their necks. Forty old people stand in the courtyard, silent, holding up their keys. The young magistrate looks at them for a long time and then, wisely, invites them all to lunch. The stores stay.

events.text: The heir you once advised has reigned for many years. Today the king's own heir must be chosen, and the king, old now, sends for you and three name tablets, and smiles. "I know," the king says. "It will not choose. But I want it to watch me choose."

choices.text: Lay the tablets in the courtyard, and let the king choose

effects.log: You lay them down. The king walks round them for an hour, talking to the ground, out loud, about each heir: what they are good at, what they are afraid of, who they listen to. Then the king picks one up. The ground under the courtyard warms, all at once, the whole courtyard, not under any one tablet. "There," the king says. "It liked being told."

choices.text: Ask the king what all those years taught

effects.log: "That the heavy days were the days I tried to carry it all myself," the king says. "And the light ones were the days I asked the council, the elders, the market grandmothers." The king picks up a tablet: the heir who argues most with the council and always comes back. "That one," the king says, "will set things down."

events.text: The great temple of the weeping statue is burning: horsemen from the steppe have reached the capital. The monks are trying to drag the statue out. It is far too heavy. Its face is wet.

choices.text: Help them move it

ok.log: You put your shoulder to it with the monks, and it moves, slowly, as if something underneath were pushing too, and you get it out through the back gate and down into the ravine before the roof comes in. It sits there for a hundred years, hidden in the brush, weeping only when it rains. Later they build a small hall round it.

fail.log: You heave and it does not move. The roof begins to fall. The monks pull you out. From outside you watch the hall burn round the statue, and its face, in the firelight, is wet, and the ground under the temple is shaking like someone sobbing. When it is over, the statue is gone. Only the warm ground remains. (-8 health)

choices.text: Get the monks out and let the statue stay

effects.log: "It does not want to leave," you tell the monks, and you make them go. The temple burns. The statue goes with it, melting, gold and iron, into the ground under the hall, and the ground takes it like a hand closing on a coin. Years later the monks dig there and find nothing at all, only earth, warm, and the faint smell of incense.

events.text: The pagoda {npc} built has stood for many years. {npc} the master builder, very old now, asks to be carried to its foot one last time, to put a hand on the centre pillar.

choices.text: Carry {npc} there

effects.log: You carry {npc} through the temple gate and set {npc} down at the foot of the centre pillar. {npc} lays one old hand on the wood. "Still true," {npc} says. "Every joint. It held them for me." {npc} sits there till dark, talking quietly to the pillar about the old kingdom in the west, and you sit a little way off and keep watch.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what holds a pagoda up

effects.log: "Not the pillar," {npc} says. "Not the joints. Not the relics. The ground. A building is a question you ask the ground, and if the ground says yes, it stands." {npc} pats the pillar. "This ground said yes to an enemy. I have never got over it."

events.text: {npc}, the archer who crossed on the turtles' backs, is a king now, and old, and dying. {npc} asks you to come at dawn to the hill east of the capital. "It will come," {npc} says. "I asked it to, long ago. Will you carry me up?"

choices.text: Carry {npc} up the hill

effects.log: You carry {npc} up the hill on your back, as light as a child now. At the top the clouds over the east turn gold, and part, and something vast and golden comes down out of them, slowly, with its head bowed, and stops above the grass. {npc} climbs onto its head, by some last strength, and turns, and lifts one hand to you. Then they rise together into the dawn.

choices.text: Say goodbye at the foot of the hill, and let {npc} climb alone

effects.log: "This part is yours," you say. {npc} nods, and climbs, very slowly, alone, the way {npc} once crossed a river alone. At the top the clouds go gold. You do not see what comes down. You see only, after a while, a gold light rising from the hilltop into the east, and the grass on the hill bowing all one way.

events.text: Long after the burning, a king of a new dynasty wants to rebuild the nine-storey pagoda on the old foundation stones. The court is excited. The architects are already measuring. You were there the night it burned.

choices.text: Say: build it somewhere new; let the old stones rest

effects.log: "Let the old stones rest," you say. "Whatever held it up has earned its sleep." The king is disappointed, and then thoughtful, and the new pagoda is built on a hill a day's ride away. The sixty-four stones stay in the grass, and the socket stays full of rainwater, and children climb on them on summer evenings, and the stones are warm.

choices.text: Say: ask the ground first

effects.log: "Ask the ground," you say. The king, amused, sets a single post in the centre socket overnight. In the morning it is lying flat in the grass, neatly, as if laid down by a careful hand. The king laughs, and lays it back down himself, and builds elsewhere. Some questions, the king says, only need asking once.

events.text: You have come back to the river mouth on the East Sea, years after the bell went in. A storm is coming. The fishermen are hauling their boats up the shingle, and an old one says: "Stay tonight. You will hear it."

choices.text: Stay, and listen

effects.log: You stay. At midnight, under the roar of the waves, there it is: a deep, slow note, from under the sea, rising and falling with the storm. The fishermen do not even look up from their mending. "It rings when the sea is wild," the old one says, "so the boats know where the river mouth is." You sit on the shingle in the rain till dawn.

choices.text: Row out in the morning calm and look down

ok.log: In the glassy morning you row out over the river mouth and look down. Far below, in green water, something huge and round lies on the sand, and coiled around it, faint and gold and enormous, something else, asleep. You row back very quietly. You tell nobody, ever.

fail.log: You row out over the river mouth and look down into green water and see only sand and weed. But your oar, dipping, strikes something deep down that rings, very faintly, like a struck bell, and the whole boat hums. You row back with the hair standing up on your arms.

events.text: The crown that the ministers once tried to give the Yellow Dragon has been kept in a box in the treasury ever since. Now a young usurper has seized the capital and wants it, "the crown the dragon touched", to make the seizure legitimate.

choices.text: Get to the treasury first and take it away

ok.log: You get into the treasury and out with the box. When you open it, far from the capital, the crown inside has turned to yellow clay, perfectly crown-shaped, warm. You laugh until you have to sit down. The usurper never gets it. The usurper does not last the year.

fail.log: The usurper's guard catch you in the treasury. The usurper takes the box and opens it before the whole court. Inside is a crown-shaped lump of yellow clay, warm, crumbling. The court is very quiet. The usurper does not last the year. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the usurper open the box

effects.log: You let it happen. The usurper opens the box in the throne hall in front of everyone, and inside is not a crown but a fist-sized lump of warm yellow clay. Somebody at the back of the court laughs. Then everybody does. A usurper can survive a great many things, but not that, and the usurper is gone by spring.

events.text: A small boy in your village, born the year you saw the centre filled, has drawn a picture in the dirt of the threshing yard: a circle, four marks round it, and a big coiled shape in the middle. "I dreamed it," the boy says. "Is it true?"

choices.text: Say yes, and tell him what you saw

effects.log: You sit down on the yard and tell him everything: the cloud terrace, the four banners, the light gathering in the middle. He listens with his mouth open. When you finish he goes very quiet, and then puts his hand flat on his picture, in the middle, and says, "It is warm." It is.

choices.text: Say: draw it again, but bigger

effects.log: "Draw it bigger," you say. He draws it all across the yard, the circle and the four marks and the coil, and the other children come and help, and by sunset the whole threshing yard is a picture of the centre of heaven. That night it rains, and the picture washes out, and in the morning the yard is green in the middle.

events.text: Many people in the world below now carry a little of the weight, a household or a village at a time, without knowing each other. Tonight, on the bare hilltop where you first offered, you find a dozen of them sitting in the dark with their palms on the earth.

choices.text: Sit down among them

effects.log: You sit down among them. Nobody speaks. The ground under all of you is warm, and quiet, and for the first time since you have known it, it does not feel tired. It feels, if anything, rested, like a field left fallow for a year. Near dawn a farmer beside you whispers: "It is lighter tonight." You nod. It is.

choices.text: Leave them, and go home lighter

effects.log: You leave them to it. Walking home, you realise you have not been carrying anything for a long time, and that it was handed on so gently you did not notice. You sleep on the bare earth of your own yard that night, out of old habit. It is warm, and asks nothing of you.

events.text: The Jade court has created a new office: Keeper of Things That Need No Keeping. They have offered it to you, after your report on the centre. It comes with a desk, a seal, and nothing whatever to do.

choices.text: Accept, and do nothing, beautifully

effects.log: You accept. For a century you sit at the desk and do nothing, beautifully, and once a year you go and stand at the empty middle of the guardians' terrace and say "All well," and it is. The other offices of heaven are first scornful, then envious, then quietly copy you.

choices.text: Decline, and suggest they give it to a farmer

effects.log: "Give it to a farmer," you say, "one who changes the rice in the jar every tenth month." The court is baffled, but desperate, and does. The farmer, an immortal of the lowest rank, takes the office very seriously and changes the rice in a jar behind the Jade court's kitchens every tenth month. Heaven has its best harvest in a thousand years.

events.text: The clerks of the almanac have finished a new calendar for heaven, and in it, for the first time, the eighteen days before each season are written in yellow ink, not left blank. They have asked you to present it to the centre.

choices.text: Carry it to the empty middle of the terrace and lay it down

effects.log: You lay the scroll in the middle of the guardians' terrace. The cloud under it warms, and the yellow ink glows, and something vast and quiet seems to read it, slowly, every line, the way an old farmer reads a new almanac, unimpressed and secretly pleased. In the morning the scroll is gone, and in its place a single grain of rice.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the four banners first

effects.log: You read it aloud, all of it, to the four banners at the four sides. At each yellow passage, each banner dips, in turn, east, south, west, north, as if handing something over. When you reach the end, the middle of the terrace is warm, and the clerks, who have never seen the banners bow, are weeping into their sleeves.

events.text: {npc}, once a king carried up from the eastern hill, has decided to go back down. Not to rule: to be born again, as a farmer, on the hill. "I want to change the rice in a jar," {npc} says. "I never once did it, as a king."
events.arc: The King from the Eastern Hill

choices.text: Walk {npc} to the edge of heaven

effects.log: You walk {npc} to the very edge of the terraces. {npc} looks down at the hill, and laughs, and steps off, lightly, like a child jumping into a stream. Years later, on a visit below, you pass a farmhouse at the foot of the eastern hill where a child is changing the rice in the jar behind the house, very solemnly, talking to it. You do not stop. You smile all the way home.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to stay one more century

effects.log: "One more century," you ask. {npc} considers, and stays, and spends it teaching you to grow rice in yellow earth on a cloud, badly, with great enjoyment. At the end of the century {npc} goes down anyway. The rice you grow afterwards is not very good. You grow it every year.

events.text: The young king is building a new palace east of the moon-fortress, on low marshy ground, and every village in the district has sent labourers. You are one of them, up to the waist in black mud, cutting drains. This morning, where your spade goes in, the mud turns warm and then, unmistakably, gold.

choices.text: Call the overseer

effects.log: The overseer comes, swearing, and looks, and stops swearing. By noon there is a crowd on the bank: officials, then monks, then, at dusk, the young king, who wades into the mud in royal silk to see. The gold light is spreading under the whole site like dawn under water. The king stands there a long time without a word.

choices.text: Keep digging, quietly

effects.log: You keep digging. Everywhere your spade goes the mud is warm. By the end of the day the whole crew has noticed, and nobody says anything, and the drains you cut that week run so clean and so fast that the marsh is dry in a month, which the engineers swear is impossible.

events.text: The foundation stones of the new palace are being laid. On the morning of the laying, the whole crew is on the site when the ground under the marsh rises, a hand's breadth, everywhere at once, and something huge and golden lifts out of the mud between the stones, and looks at the young king, and goes back down.

choices.text: Throw yourself flat

effects.log: You throw yourself flat in the mud with everyone else. When you dare to look up, the young king is the only one still standing, very pale, staring at the place it went down. That evening a herald announces that the palace will not be built. A temple will stand here instead, named for what rose out of the marsh.

choices.text: Stand, and look at it

effects.log: You stand. You see it: a golden head the size of a house, two eyes like harvest moons, looking not at the king but at the stones, the foundation, the shape of the thing about to be built on its back. It seems to think about it. Then it sinks, slowly, like a farmer lying back down after checking the field. The palace becomes a temple. You are not surprised.

events.text: The temple on the old marsh is finished, and named for the dragon that rose there, and you, one of the labourers who dug its drains, have been invited by the monks to the dedication, as a witness to what was seen.

choices.text: Tell the monks exactly what you saw

effects.log: You tell it as it was: the warm mud, the gold, the head, the eyes looking at the stones. An old monk writes it down. "It looked at the stones," the monk repeats. "Not the king." The monk thinks about that for a long time, and in the end makes it the first line of the temple's founding record.

choices.text: Go round the back and put a hand on the ground

effects.log: While the dedication goes on with drums and banners, you slip round the back of the new hall and kneel and lay your hand on the earth where the marsh used to be. Warm, deep, settled, like a sleeper who has decided to stay. You say thank you, for the drains, for the dry month, for not being crushed. Something, far down, seems to say you are welcome.

events.text: {npc}, a tomb painter of the north, has hired you to hold the lamp while {npc} paints a king's burial chamber: the four guardians of the directions on the four walls, east, west, south, north. The capstone at the centre of the ceiling is still blank. "I do not know what goes in the middle," {npc} says. "The old books say nothing."

choices.text: Say: something that holds the four together

effects.log: "Something that holds the four together," you say. {npc} lies on the scaffold a long time, looking up at the blank capstone. "The centre," {npc} says at last. "Earth. Yellow." That night {npc} grinds yellow ochre for the first time in the whole job and sits with the bowl of it, not painting, just looking at the ceiling.

choices.text: Say: leave it blank

effects.log: "Leave it blank," you say. "Let the king's soul find its own middle." {npc} considers that. They leave it blank that week. And every night, when you come back with the lamp, the blank capstone is a little warmer than the walls, as if something were thinking about coming to fill it.

events.text: {npc} the tomb painter has decided: a coiled yellow dragon on the capstone, over the four guardians. But {npc} cannot get it right. Six times painted, six times scraped off. "It will not sit," {npc} says. "It keeps looking like it wants to leave."

choices.text: Hold the lamp all night and say nothing

effects.log: You hold the lamp all night. {npc} paints, and scrapes, and paints. Near dawn the lamp flickers, and {npc}'s brush moves without seeming to think, and the coil closes on itself, head to tail, round the middle of the stone. {npc} lies back on the scaffold, shaking. It sits. It is the best thing {npc} will ever paint.

choices.text: Tell {npc}: paint it asleep

effects.log: "Paint it asleep," you say. "Content. As if it has decided to stay." {npc} stares at you, then laughs, and paints it with its eyes half closed, coiled like a cat by a stove. It sits. A thousand years later, people will stand under it in lamplight and feel, for no reason they can name, that they are welcome.

events.text: Summer will not end. It is the tenth month and still hot, and the barley in the north of the province is green while in the south it is rotting gold, and between them, across the fields, runs a line as sharp as a knife cut. The farmers are terrified. The eighteen days between the seasons came and went, and nothing changed hands.
events.arc: The Season That Would Not Turn

choices.text: Walk the line from end to end

effects.log: You walk the line for three days. In the middle of the province, where it bends, you find a new lord's fortress, built on the navel of the valley in the forbidden days, its foundations driven deep into the earth. The ground there is cold. Whatever holds the seasons together has been pinned down.

choices.text: Ask the oldest farmer what to do

effects.log: The oldest farmer in the province says: "Something is sitting where it should not. Find it." Then the old farmer points with a pipe toward the middle of the province, where a new lord has been building on the round knoll in the valley's navel. You go.

events.text: The new lord's fortress sits on the navel of the valley, driven deep in the forbidden days. Under it the ground is cold. Around it, for fifty li, the seasons are stuck. The lord's guards are on the walls.
events.arc: The Season That Would Not Turn

choices.text: Go in and make the lord dig the foundations out

ok.log: You go in through the gate and through the guard captain. The lord, faced with you and a province of starving farmers at the gate, orders the deepest foundation post pulled. It comes out with a sound like a cork from a jar, and warm air comes up out of the hole, and across the province, in one afternoon, every green field goes gold.

fail.log: The guard captain stops you at the gate. But that night the ground under the fortress, which has been cold for a year, heaves once, enormously, like a sleeper throwing off a weight, and the deepest foundation post comes up out of the earth by itself, and the fortress cracks in half. By morning, every green field in the province is gold. (-12 health)

choices.text: Sit outside the walls on the bare earth, and wait with it

effects.log: You sit on the bare earth outside the walls for nine days and nights, palms flat on the ground, keeping the cold company. On the tenth day the lord, unnerved by the strange figure who does not eat, comes out to ask what you want. "Pull the post," you say. The lord, to be rid of you, does. The province turns gold by evening.

events.text: Once in a thousand years heaven holds the Rite of the Five Directions: immortals in blue, red, white and black stand at the four sides, and one in yellow stands in the middle. The one in yellow is chosen by lot. This millennium, the lot has fallen on you.
events.arc: The Rite of the Five Directions

choices.text: Stand in the middle and do nothing at all

effects.log: You stand in the middle in yellow and do nothing at all, which is the hardest thing you have ever done in heaven. Around you the four colours dance, and you are their still point. When the rite ends, the four step in, one by one, and bow, not to you but to the ground you are standing on, and you feel it warm under your feet, pleased.

choices.text: Decline the lot and ask who belongs there

effects.log: "I am not the centre," you say. "Who is?" The four colours stop. Nobody has ever declined the lot. Then the master of the rite, very old, smiles. "Then we will leave the middle empty," the master says, "and see who comes." The rite is held around an empty yellow place. At the end, it is glowing.

events.text: After the Rite of the Five Directions, the yellow robe you wore, or did not wear, has been sent to you, folded. It is heavy. Far heavier than silk should be.
events.arc: The Rite of the Five Directions

choices.text: Put it on, once, alone

effects.log: You put it on, alone, in your hall. It is like putting on a whole country: every harvest, every road, every quarrel, leaning in. You stand under it until you understand it is not asking you to carry it, only to know what it weighs. Then you take it off, fold it, and send it back to the middle of the terrace, where it belongs.

choices.text: Lay it on the ground of the world below, in a farmyard

effects.log: You take it down to the world below and lay it, folded, in the yard of a farmhouse at the first full moon, and leave before anyone sees. In the morning the family finds nothing but a square of yellow earth, warm, where the frost has melted. That year their band stamps on the yard, and the yard stamps back.

events.text: The village shaman plants the five flags for the autumn rite: blue to the east, white to the west, red to the south, black to the north, and yellow in the middle. Every year the yellow flag droops. This year it stands up straight in a dead calm, and the earth round its pole is warm enough to steam in the cold night air.

choices.text: Kneel by the yellow flag and put a hand on the earth

effects.log: Warm, and steady, the way a hearthstone is steady long after the fire. Around you the four flags flutter in a wind you cannot feel, and the yellow one does not move at all. The shaman watches you a long time, and then says, quietly, that the old people always said the middle would be filled one day. "It seems it was," the shaman says.

choices.text: Ask the shaman why the middle flag stands

effects.log: "Somebody sits in the middle now," says the shaman, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. "The four used to quarrel all year. Now they quarrel and then they agree. You can tell from the weather." You think about the weather. It has, now you think of it, been very sensible for years.

events.text: A drought threatens, and the county's four great families have fallen out over the water: the east wants it for rice, the west for orchards, the south for the mill, the north for the salt pans. They have asked you, of all people, to stand in the middle of the market square while they shout.

choices.text: Stand in the middle and say nothing until they agree

effects.log: You stand there all afternoon. The ground under your feet is warm. The shouting goes round you and round you and slowly runs out, the way a top runs out, and toward sunset the four heads of family find they have divided the water fairly without quite meaning to. Nobody can say what you did. You are not sure yourself.

choices.text: Ask each family one question, the same one

effects.log: "If you were the others," you ask each in turn, "what would you want?" It is a simple question. It takes them a day to answer it. By evening the water is shared. That night you dream of four banners on a terrace of cloud, and in the middle something gold, asleep, which is not asleep, and says "Good."

events.text: The oldest woman on the lane says that for as long as anyone remembers the seasons here have handed over like polite guests: spring never overstays, autumn never barges in. This year, in the eighteen days before autumn, you are out in the field alone, and the air goes still and gold, and for one breath you feel the whole year turn round you.
events.arc: The Year That Knows What It Is Doing

choices.text: Stand very still and let it turn

effects.log: It turns: summer handing itself to autumn, unhurried, through the ground under your feet. For one breath you know where every harvest in the land is, and what it weighs, and that it will be enough. Then it is only a field again, and a little cooler. You walk home and do not tell anyone, because how would you?

choices.text: Bow to the middle of the field

effects.log: You bow, feeling foolish, to nothing, to the middle of a barley field. The stillness answers the way an old person answers a child's bow, with a small, pleased nod you feel rather than see. The harvest that year weighs exactly what the farmers hoped. Not more. Exactly.

events.text: At harvest the county's tax clerk comes with new measures, and the village holds its breath. The measures are set on the old scale in the threshing yard. Before anyone can lean on it, the scale settles level by itself, and stays there, and the clerk's face goes from smug to thoughtful.
events.arc: The Year That Knows What It Is Doing

choices.text: Ask the clerk to weigh one sack, slowly, for everyone

effects.log: One sack, slowly, in front of the whole village. The measure is honest. The clerk looks almost relieved. "In this county," the clerk admits, "the scales do not let you cheat. Nobody knows why. My predecessor tried for years and went home with a bad back."

choices.text: Pour a handful of the new rice on the ground first

effects.log: You pour a handful of new rice on the bare earth of the yard, the way the old people do, for whatever holds the year together. The earth is warm. The clerk raises an eyebrow and then, after a moment, does the same. The weighing goes quickly and fairly, and the clerk stays for supper.

events.text: High in the hills there is a pool under a waterfall that never freezes, not in the worst winter. The hunters say the bedrock under it is warm, and that something once climbed out of it into the sky, and that something else went down under it so that the first could rise. You have walked a long way to see it.

choices.text: Put your hand flat on the warm rock under the water

effects.log: The rock is warm as a sleeping animal, and patient, and very deep. You stay until your arm is numb with the cold water above and warm through with the stone below. You come away feeling as if you have been allowed, for a moment, to stand on someone's shoulders.

choices.text: Leave an offering of rice on the bank and go

effects.log: You leave a little bag of new rice on a flat stone by the pool, and bow, and go. When you look back from the ridge, the steam over the water has risen into a long shape, climbing, and under it the pool is shining gold. Then it is only steam.

events.text: A child from your village has fallen into the warm pool in the hills, and come out again laughing, and says the water carried them up from the very bottom, "like somebody lifting." The village elders want to fence the pool off.

choices.text: Talk them out of the fence

effects.log: "Something under that pool makes room," you say. "It always has. A fence will only teach the children to climb." The elders grumble and agree. The pool stays open. Every child in the village learns to swim in it, and not one ever drowns.

choices.text: Let them fence it, and keep a gate in the fence

effects.log: You build the fence with them, and leave a gate, and nobody locks it. That autumn, in the eighteen days before the season, a long ripple goes up the waterfall from the pool, against the current, and the whole village sees it. Nobody mentions the fence again.

events.text: There is a saying in the old capital: get up before dawn on the hill east of the city, and on a clear morning you will see two of them, a king and the thing that carries the king, crossing the sunrise. Nobody you know has seen it. You climb the hill on a clear morning, on a whim.

choices.text: Wait until the sun is all the way up

effects.log: Just as the sun clears the hills, something long and gold goes across it, low, unhurried, and on its head a small upright figure in court robes, looking down at the city with great fondness.
