Then it is gone into the light. You come down the hill shaking, and laughing, and you never tell anyone who would not believe you.

choices.text: Bow to the east before the sun comes up

effects.log: You bow to the east in the grey light, the way the old people of the lane do. When you straighten, the sunrise is just beginning, and the wind on the hill is warm, the way a breath is warm, and for a moment you feel looked at, kindly, by two people at once.

events.text: A descendant of the old founding house, very poor now, lives at the foot of the eastern hill selling straw sandals. Every dawn they climb the hill and bow. A rich man from the capital wants to buy the hill to build a summer villa on it.

choices.text: Help the sandal seller fight the sale

effects.log: You go to the magistrate with the sandal seller and the old annals, and argue for three days. The magistrate reads the line about the king who went up from the hill, and refuses the sale. On the morning you win, the sunrise over the hill is the brightest anyone in the city can remember.

choices.text: Buy a pair of sandals and climb the hill with them

effects.log: You buy a pair of sandals and climb with the seller at dawn, and bow beside them. The seller tells you the story of the founder, badly and lovingly. The rich man's villa is never built: the ground on the hill will not take a foundation post. It simply will not.

events.text: You are at the great ruined temple site with the sixty-four stones in the grass. Children jump from stone to stone. An old farmer rests a cow in the shade. In the middle the centre stone's socket is full of rainwater, though it has not rained in a month, and the farmer says it never dries.

choices.text: Sit on the centre stone for a while

effects.log: You sit. The stone is warm. After a long while you notice that it rises under you, very slightly, and falls, and rises: slow as a sleeper. The children's feet thump from stone to stone around you, and you have the strangest feeling that something under all sixty-four of them is enjoying it.

choices.text: Join the children and jump the stones

effects.log: You jump the stones with the children, all sixty-four, and fall off twice. The farmer laughs. When you reach the centre stone the water in the socket shivers, as if something underneath had laughed too. You go home with grass stains and a lightness you cannot account for.

events.text: Builders have come to the ruined temple site with carts: a new county office needs foundation stones, and these are good ones, already cut. The old farmer with the cow is standing in front of the centre stone with a hoe.

choices.text: Stand beside the farmer

effects.log: You stand beside the farmer. The builders laugh, and then try to lever up the first stone, and it will not move. Not one of the sixty-four will move, not with ten men on the bar. In the end the builders go and quarry their own. The farmer offers you a turn holding the cow.

choices.text: Tell the builders what the stones held up

effects.log: You tell them about the nine storeys, the lightning, the horsemen, and the thing that stayed under the stones when everything burned. The foreman listens with his cap in his hands. Then he takes his carts away empty, and that evening comes back alone to pour a cup of wine into the centre socket.

events.text: In this kingdom, the old people say, there was once a dragon under the throne, and it gave away its burdens one by one until it had nothing left to carry, and then it went, and nobody noticed. The elders under the zelkova still meet every month and decide things. Today they have asked you to sit with them.

choices.text: Sit, and listen more than you speak

effects.log: You sit, and listen. The elders argue about a ditch, a debt and a widow's field, and decide all three fairly by sunset, and nobody asks a magistrate or a king or a god. You realise that this is what the dragon left: not luck, but the habit of deciding well. It is the most valuable thing you have ever been near.

choices.text: Bring them a quarrel nobody else could settle

effects.log: You bring them the quarrel between your family and the next over the boundary stone, which has lasted three generations. The elders hear both sides and settle it in an afternoon. Old Cho of the lane, who has hated the neighbours for forty years, goes home bewildered and oddly happy.

events.text: The new king is young and nervous, and on the morning of the coronation sends for anyone in the capital who remembers how the kingdom is supposed to be ruled. The palace is full of scholars with long speeches. You have been sent for too, because your village is famous for its elders.

choices.text: Tell the young king: share it, every year a little

effects.log: "Every year give one thing away," you say. "A decision to the elders, a measure to the market, a road to the county. Keep only what you cannot give." The young king writes it on a slip of paper and keeps it in a sleeve for years. The reign is long and quiet.

choices.text: Tell the young king: you will hardly be needed

effects.log: "Forgive me," you say, "but you will hardly be needed. The kingdom knows how." The court gasps. The young king laughs, for the first time that day, out of sheer relief. It is, the annals later say, the happiest coronation in the history of the house.

events.text: Behind your family's old farmhouse, beside the soy-sauce jars, there is a little rice jar with a straw cap. The oldest woman on the lane changes the rice every tenth month and bows to it. In the hardest frost the jar is warm. This year her knees are bad, and the basket of new rice has been handed to you.
events.arc: The Jar That Is Always Warm

choices.text: Change the rice and bow, the way you have seen it done

effects.log: You lift the cap. The old rice is warm, warm as if just steamed, and smells of new straw. You pour in the new, and straighten the cap, and bow, awkwardly. Under your knees the ground goes warmer, contented. The oldest woman on the lane, watching from the step, nods once, and does not need to say anything.

choices.text: Ask the jar, quietly, how long it has been there

effects.log: You ask it, feeling foolish. Nothing answers. But that night you dream of a house site in the dead days before autumn, a spade going in, warm clay, and a hundred tenth months, one after another, and every one of them someone of your family kneeling where you knelt. You wake up warm.

events.text: Your family has to sell the old farmhouse. Debts. The buyer is decent enough, but the house has to be empty by the new moon, and the little rice jar behind it, with its straw cap, is the last thing left.
events.arc: The Jar That Is Always Warm

choices.text: Leave the jar where it is, for the new family

effects.log: You leave it, and tell the new family how to change the rice. They listen politely and you can see they think it is a peasant's superstition. But the next tenth month the new wife of the house comes to find you in town, red-eyed, to say the jar was warm in the frost, and to ask what to say to it.

choices.text: Dig it up carefully and take it with you

effects.log: You dig it up with your hands, very carefully, and carry it to the new house wrapped in a quilt. You bury it behind the new kitchen with the straw cap over it. For a month it is cold, and you are frightened. Then, on the first frost, it is warm again. Something has followed the family, and not the house.

events.text: Farmers ploughing on the hill have broken into an old stone tomb, and the magistrate has sent you in with a lamp to see whether it is worth guarding. On the four walls, faded, the guardians of the four directions. And on the capstone overhead, in the centre of the ceiling, a coil of gold that catches the lamp like fresh paint.

choices.text: Lie down on the floor and look up at it

effects.log: You lie on the cold floor where the sleeper once lay, and look up. The coil of gold looks down. It is asleep, or nearly, eyes half shut, coiled like a cat by a stove. You stay an hour and come out feeling as if someone had kept watch over you, too, for that hour.

choices.text: Write a report that it must be guarded

effects.log: You write the report that night, by the same lamp: four walls, four guardians, and a centre of gold that must never be touched. The magistrate reads it twice and sets a guard on the hill. The farmers plough round the tomb for a hundred years.

events.text: A gang of tomb robbers has been caught on the hill with the old painted tomb. They are terrified, and want to confess to someone: they got as far as the inner chamber, lifted the lamp, and ran. You have been asked to take down what they say.

choices.text: Ask them what they saw

effects.log: "It opened its eyes," the leader says, white to the lips. "The gold one on the ceiling. It opened its eyes and looked at the sleeper, and then at us, the way a farmer looks at a fox." You write it down exactly. The magistrate lets them go with a warning, since nothing was taken, and they become, you hear, very honest men.

choices.text: Take them back to the tomb to put the stones back

effects.log: You make them put back every stone they moved, by daylight, with you watching. At the inner door the leader stops and will not go in. You go in alone with the lamp. The gold in the ceiling is quiet and half asleep. You bow to it. The leader, outside, bows to the door.

events.text: You are out with the fishing boats at the river mouth when a storm catches the fleet. The old fishermen do not seem afraid. "Listen," one says. And under the wind, under the waves, deep down, a great bell is ringing, slow and steady, as if to say: here is the harbour, here.

choices.text: Steer toward the sound

effects.log: You steer toward it. The bell rings, and rings, and the black water opens into the calm of the harbour mouth exactly where the sound is loudest. Every boat comes home. On the beach the old fisherman says that the bell went down with the invaders' ship centuries ago, and something gold went down with it, and they keep each other company.

choices.text: Ask the old fisherman about the bell

effects.log: "The horsemen dragged it over the low pass," the old fisherman shouts over the wind, "to put it on a ship. The ship went down right here. And something went down with it, to hold it." The bell rings. The boats turn toward it like geese. You come home with a story you will tell your whole life.

events.text: A diver from the capital has come to the river mouth with ropes and a raft, hired to bring up the great bell for a rich temple. The fishermen are furious. The diver has asked you, as someone who has heard it ring, where exactly it lies.

choices.text: Refuse to tell

effects.log: "Ask the fishermen," you say, knowing they will not tell either. The diver searches all summer and finds only mud and a warm current, warmer than it should be, that pushes the raft gently back toward the shore every time. In autumn the diver goes home, and on the first storm the bell rings as always.

choices.text: Take the diver out in a storm to hear it

effects.log: You take the diver out on a stormy night. The bell rings under the waves, and the boats turn toward it, and come home. The diver sits on the beach afterwards for a long time. "I could not bring that up," the diver says at last. "Who would ring for them then?" The raft is sold for firewood.

events.text: The old throne hall of the last kings is a museum of dust now. You have been given a night watch in it. In the dark the golden chair stands empty on its dais, and above it, painted in the ceiling, the gold dragon looks down. Toward midnight you would swear it is looking at the chair the way a dog looks at a door.

choices.text: Sweep the dais, quietly, before dawn

effects.log: You sweep the dust from the dais and wipe the golden chair, very carefully, the way you would tidy a room for someone who is not coming back. When you look up, the dragon in the ceiling seems a little less sad. Probably the light. You do it every night of your watch after that.

choices.text: Count the claws on the painted dragon

effects.log: Seven. Seven claws, which the old painters argued about for a hundred years. You count them twice by lantern light. Then, absurdly, you bow, because something about seven claws over an empty chair makes you want to say sorry to someone.

events.text: A foreign envoy touring the old palace stands under the dragon ceiling and laughs at the empty golden chair: a small kingdom, a large chair, a short empire. The guides have gone red and silent.

choices.text: Tell the envoy what the chair was for

effects.log: "A king sat there," you say, "so that the world would know this country stood on its own ground, if only for a little while." The envoy stops laughing. Above you the gold dragon looks down at the chair. The envoy, after a moment, takes off a hat and bows to it, and you think that will do.

choices.text: Say nothing, and look up

effects.log: You say nothing and look up at the ceiling. One by one the others look up too, the guides, the envoy's clerks, the envoy. The dragon looks down at all of them over the empty chair. The silence goes on until it is a kind of answer. The envoy leaves without another word.

events.text: Your county lies in the middle of the land, and it is the only county with no weather of its own: storms come to it from five directions, in five colours of cloud, and quarrel over it, and leave. The old people say that once something sat in the middle and held them together, and it broke.

choices.text: Climb the ridge and watch the five storms

effects.log: From the ridge you can see them all: a blue rain in the east, a red heat in the south, a white frost in the west, a black wind in the north, and a yellow dust wandering lost between them. None of them comes to the middle. For a moment you feel, very clearly, that the middle is waiting to be held, and that it is not your job, and that someone should do it.

choices.text: Plant a yellow flag in the middle of the county

effects.log: You plant a yellow flag on the bare hill in the middle of the county, the way the shamans do. Nothing happens. But that summer, for the first time anyone remembers, two of the storms meet over the county and rain together, gently, instead of fighting. It is a start.

events.text: A yellow dust storm has come down on your village out of season, and inside it, the children swear, there was a long dim shape like a lost dog, going round and round the village well as if looking for something.

choices.text: Go out into the dust and call to it

effects.log: You go out into the dust with a cloth over your face and call to it, the way you would call a lost animal. The dust slows. For a moment something huge and dim and yellow lies down round the well, tired, and the dust settles over the fields like a blanket. In the morning the soil is richer than it has been in a hundred years.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of clean water at the well

effects.log: You leave a bowl of clean water on the well-stone for it. In the morning the bowl is empty and full of fine yellow earth, and the storm is gone, and the barley comes up thicker in your field than anyone else's. You leave a bowl out every year after that.

events.text: Three days' walk from your village lies the old capital that sank: half its walls under the earth, nothing growing, not a weed in three hundred years, the palace well silent. People avoid it. You are crossing it because the road round is twice as long, and the ground under your feet is very, very heavy.

choices.text: Stop at the silent well and pour your water in

effects.log: You pour your whole water skin into the dry well. It is a stupid thing to do with two days to walk. Far down you hear it land, and then, very faintly, a sound like a long breath let out after holding it a very long time. When you walk on, the ground feels a little lighter. Probably you are only tired.

choices.text: Walk on quickly, without looking back

effects.log: You walk quickly and do not look back, but the heaviness follows you to the edge of the ruin, like an old dog that cannot leave its yard. At the edge you stop, and turn, and say, "I am sorry," without knowing why. The heaviness lies down. You go on.

events.text: Word comes that a single shoot of barley has come up in the old sunk capital, in the crack of a palace foundation stone, the first green thing in three hundred years. Half the county has gone to look. Some want to build a shrine round it.

choices.text: Go and ask them to leave it alone

effects.log: "Do not put a roof over it," you say. "It has had enough weight." They argue, and listen, and in the end build nothing. By the next spring there are a dozen shoots, and the palace well has water in it, a hand's depth, cold and sweet. The capital is beginning, very slowly, to set something down.

choices.text: Help them build a low fence and nothing more

effects.log: A fence knee-high, nothing heavier, so nobody treads on it. You carry the poles yourself. When the last one is in, the ground under your feet seems to shift, as if something enormous had moved its weight from one side to the other, more comfortably. That summer the ruin goes green in patches.

events.text: In your province nobody wears yellow. Not at weddings, not at funerals, not a ribbon. The old people say a tyrant once had a golden dragon sewn into his robe and carved over his gate, and when his capital burned, the yellow burned with it, and the colour has never been forgiven. A cloth merchant has just offered you a bolt.

choices.text: Refuse the yellow silk

effects.log: You refuse it. The merchant shrugs and puts it away. But that night you dream of a robe burning, and of something gold inside it that did not want to be there, that had stayed too long out of loyalty and could not get out. You wake with a terrible sadness that is not yours.

choices.text: Buy it, and wear a yellow ribbon openly

effects.log: You buy it and wear a yellow ribbon to the market. People step back from you. A child cries. An old man spits. And one old woman, very slowly, comes up and touches the ribbon, and says: "It was not the colour's fault, you know. It was the man." She goes away weeping.

events.text: Ploughing near the old burned capital, a farmer has turned up a charred scrap of yellow silk with half a gold dragon embroidered on it. Nobody will touch it. The village headman wants it burned again, properly, with a rite. They have asked you, since you are not afraid of yellow.

choices.text: Bury it in clean earth instead

effects.log: You carry it out to a fallow field and bury it in clean yellow earth, and say a few words: that it is finished, that it may rest. The ground over it is warm by evening. The next spring, in that field, the barley comes up a pure gold that nobody is afraid of.

choices.text: Wash it in the river and fold it

effects.log: You wash the soot out of it in the river, slowly, until the half dragon is clean gold again, and fold it, and give it to the village temple to keep. The monks hang it in a dark corner. Over the years, the children stop being afraid of it, and then of the colour, a little.

events.text: You are in the county archive on an errand, and today the old keeper has shown you a locked box: inside it, a jade seal carved with a coiled dragon. "The Yellow Dragon Seal," the keeper whispers. "Every cruel decree of the old dynasties was stamped with it. It is priceless. Nobody who uses it is ever happy again."

choices.text: Close the box and lock it again

effects.log: You close the box. Just before the lid comes down you would swear the jade dragon moves, very slightly, as if to watch you go. The keeper locks it and gives you the key, since you were the one who closed it. The key is warm. You keep it on a string round your neck and never once open the box.

choices.text: Put your hand on the seal, gently

effects.log: You touch it. It is not cold, as jade should be, but warm, and heavy, heavier than a stone that size can be, and under the weight, very faint, there is something like a held breath, waiting to be let go. You take your hand away. You understand that it does not want to stamp anything ever again.

events.text: A magistrate's man has come to the archive with orders to take the Yellow Dragon Seal to the capital: a new minister wants it to stamp a decree of confiscation. You hold the key.

choices.text: Refuse to give up the key

ok.log: You refuse, and when the magistrate's man reaches for the key, you put him on the floor. He goes back empty-handed and furious. The decree is never stamped. The seal stays in its box, and that winter, the old keeper says, the box was warm as a sleeping cat.

fail.log: He takes the key from you by force. But when he opens the box, the seal will not lift: it is as heavy as a millstone, and three men cannot shift it. He goes back without it, and the decree is never stamped. You nurse your bruises and feel the key's string, still round your neck, warm. (-8 health)

choices.text: Give him the key, and pray the seal refuses

effects.log: You give him the key. In the capital, they say, the new minister pressed the seal on the decree, and lifted it, and the paper was blank: no red mark at all, only a faint warm smell of yellow clay. The decree was torn up. The seal came back to the archive in its box, and you put it away, and lock it, and breathe again.

events.text: Late summer, the eighteen days before autumn, and your neighbour is putting up a house in spite of the old people. You are helping dig the first post-hole. In the middle of the site the spade turns up a fist of yellow clay that is warm, warm as bread, and when you pick it up it beats, once, in your palm.

choices.text: Put it back gently and fill the hole

effects.log: You put it back, gently, exactly where it was, and fill the hole with your hands, and make your neighbour dig the post a step to the left. He grumbles. Under the new house the ground is warm all winter, and you have the strangest feeling that something down there remembers a great deal, and is starting again, and is glad of the quiet.

choices.text: Hold it until it stops beating

effects.log: You hold it in both hands. It beats, slowly, again and again, and for a moment you see things: a crossroads, a market, a palace on a marsh, a terrace of cloud with four banners round it. Then it is only warm clay. You put it back. You know, without knowing how, that it has done all this before, and chosen to do it again.

events.text: The house your neighbour built over the warm clay has had years of luck: no fire, no fever, the rice jar never empty. Now a geomancer has come to the gate, very pale, asking who dug the first post-hole in the forbidden days.

choices.text: Say it was you, and ask what it means

effects.log: "It means," the geomancer says, "that something very old has come back to the beginning. To the clay. Be kind to this house, and it will be the luck of this house for as long as it likes." Then the geomancer bows to the ground, not to you, and goes on down the road.

choices.text: Say nobody dug in the forbidden days

effects.log: "Nobody," you say. The geomancer smiles, and does not believe you, and does not mind. "Then nobody will mind," the geomancer says, "if I leave this." A small jar of new rice with a straw cap, set by the gate. You bury it in the middle of the yard that evening. The ground is warm.
